Consumer complaint narrative: On approximately XX/XX/year>, Citibank , N.A . unilaterally and without adequate advance notice closed my personal checking account. The stated reason was that I had filed what Citibank deemed to be an excessive number of transaction disputes. At the time of closure, the account held a positive balance of approximately {$6000.00} funds that are legally and rightfully mine. Upon closure, Citibank representatives informed me that my remaining balance would be disbursed via physical check mailed to my address of record, and that this process would take 30 to 60 days. I was offered no alternative disbursement method no electronic transfer, no ACH payment, no wire transfer, and no option for in-branch pickup or expedited delivery. The sole option presented was to wait up to two months to receive my own money. As of the date of this complaint XX/XX/year>, which is 24 days after account closure I have received neither my funds nor any written communication from Citibank providing a specific disbursement date, check number, tracking number, or any other verifiable confirmation that the process is underway. Despite multiple phone calls to Citibank 's customer service and requests to speak with supervisors, I have been told repeatedly that the 3060 day timeline is " standard policy '' and that no exception, escalation, or accommodation can be made regardless of circumstances. I want to be unequivocal about the severity of my situation : the {$6000.00} that Citibank is withholding constitutes the entirety of my available liquid funds. I have no other bank accounts with accessible balances, no credit lines to draw upon, and no alternative source of immediate funds. As a direct and proximate result of Citibank 's refusal to promptly return my money, I am currently experiencing homelessness. I can not afford housing, food, transportation, medication, or other basic necessities. I am a XXXX XXXX and my ability to continue my education and meet my academic obligations is being severely jeopardized. Every additional day that Citibank retains my funds compounds the harm I am suffering. Citibank 's conduct raises serious concerns under multiple federal consumer financial protection laws and regulations : ( 1 ) UDAAP Dodd-Frank Act 1031 : Withholding a consumer 's entire account balance for 3060 days following an involuntary, bank-initiated closure constitutes an unfair practice. The injury is substantial ( homelessness, inability to meet basic needs ), not reasonably avoidable ( the consumer did not choose to close the account and was given no alternative disbursement method ), and not outweighed by any countervailing benefit to consumers or competition. ( 2 ) Electronic Fund Transfer Act / Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. 1005 ) : These provisions require good faith handling of consumer funds and establish protections for electronic fund transfers. Citibank 's refusal to offer any electronic disbursement method when the technology to do so is readily available and routinely used is inconsistent with the spirit and purpose of these protections. ( 3 ) Regulation CC / Expedited Funds Availability Act ( 12 C.F.R. 229 ) : While primarily governing deposit availability, the underlying federal policy is that consumers should have prompt access to their funds. A 3060 day hold on a consumer 's entire balance following involuntary closure is fundamentally inconsistent with this principle. ( 4 ) OCC Supervisory Guidance : The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Citibank 's primary federal regulator, has issued guidance directing national banks to handle account closures in a manner that minimizes consumer harm and ensures the timely return of funds. ( 5 ) Ohio Consumer Sales Practices Act ( Ohio Rev. Code 1345.01 et seq. ) : As a consumer residing in Ohio, I am additionally protected by state law prohibiting unfair and deceptive acts or practices in consumer transactions. I have sent Citibank a formal demand letter via certified mail, return receipt requested, demanding the immediate return of my funds and providing notice of this CFPB complaint and my intention to pursue all available regulatory and legal remedies. A copy of this demand letter is attached. I respectfully urge the CFPB to intervene immediately, direct Citibank to release my funds without further delay, and investigate whether Citibank 's blanket 3060 day disbursement policy upon involuntary account closure constitutes a systemic unfair practice affecting other consumers as well.

As detailed in my prior complaint, the events at issue did not occur in isolation. Rather, immediately following my protected consumer activityspecifically, submitting a one-star customer review and filing a CFPB complaintBank of America initiated a coordinated and escalating series of adverse actions. 

Retaliation Timeline and Notice Deficiencies On XX/XX/XXXX ( Saturday ), Bank of America sent an email targeting only my mothers account ( ending in XXXX ). That email did not state that all accounts were being frozen or closed. 

On XX/XX/XXXX ( Sunday ), a second email stated that my mothers account was permanently closed.

On XX/XX/XXXX, as a direct result of the stress and uncertainty created by these sudden actions, I was forced to cancel a scheduled physical therapy appointment and go to the bank as my first priority. 

At the branch, I was informed that my account was frozen and inaccessible. During a prolonged wait, I learned incidentally and without prior notice that my credit cards were also disabled. At that time, no written or electronic notice regarding credit card closures had been provided. 

Only after submitting additional complaints did written notices concerning credit card closures arrive by mail approximately one week later. 

Additional Evidence Documents Supplementing the Prior Complaint This supplemental submission also includes additional documentary evidence that was not previously uploaded to the CFPB portal and is now submitted as supplemental proof. 

The attached materials include : Email notifications sent by Bank of America regarding account closures ; and XXXX email delivery confirmations showing the actual dates on which Bank of Americas account and credit card closure letters were delivered to our mailbox. 

The XXXX records clearly establish that : Bank account closure letters were delivered around XX/XX/XXXX, and Credit card closure letters were delivered around XX/XX/XXXX. 

These objective, third-party records directly contradict Bank of Americas assertion that timely and complete notice was provided. The evidence demonstrates a material delay between the dates Bank of America claims notices were sent and the dates on which those notices were actually received. 

These documents are submitted to support and corroborate the previously raised claims of notice failures, delayed notification, and procedurally improper account closures, and must be considered an integral part of the prior complaint. 

Targeted Retaliation Affecting My Entire Family It is critical to note that the only account solely in my name is my small business account. All other accounts were joint accounts held with my spouse. 

Despite this, Bank of America systematically targeted me and my entire family, closing : My personal accounts, Joint accounts with my spouse, My small business account, and My mothers accounts and credit card, even though I alone was the individual who submitted the review and filed the CFPB complaint.

Human and Health Impact Throughout this process : Accounts and credit cards were frozen and closed without advance notice, Access to funds was restricted, I was forced to move accounts under extreme time pressure, Ongoing uncertainty, fragmented communication, and delayed notices caused sleepless nights, and The resulting stress significantly exacerbated my existing medical condition, increasing pain and functional impairment.

Conclusion For these reasons, the conduct described can not be characterized as a routine or neutral business decision. Instead, the evidence establishes a clear pattern of retaliation, supported by documentary proof, in violation of 12 U.S.C. 5536 ( UDAAP ) and 42 U.S.C. 12203 ( ADA anti-retaliation protections ). 

This supplemental submission, together with the attached evidence, is submitted to be read in conjunction with and as an inseparable part of my prior CFPB complaint.

Sub-issue: Problem using a debit or ATM card
Consumer complaint narrative:
Between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/year>, XXXX unauthorized ATM withdrawals totaling {$2400.00} were made from my checking account over XXXX consecutive days. The withdrawals occurred in rapid succession, with each transaction approximately XXXX minute apart, including multiple {$300.00} withdrawals within minutes, and this same pattern was repeated on each of the XXXX consecutive days. 

I discovered the unauthorized activity late evening on XX/XX/year>, when a debit transaction was declined because the series of withdrawals had fully depleted my account. Early on XX/XX/year>, I promptly reported the unauthorized withdrawals to Chase. 

Despite these facts, Chase denied my theft report within XXXX day of my report and did not provide a substantive explanation or documentation supporting its determination, stating only that Chase determined the transactions were authorized based solely on the use of the correct PIN, without providing supporting documentation or analysis. I explained that I did not authorize the transactions, that I had never used an ATM withdrawal on this account, and that my PIN had been compromised. 

Chase later advised that the disputed withdrawals were conducted using electronically captured card information that was provisioned to a mobile device ( an XXXX ) and then used to complete the ATM transactions, rather than by me using my physical card. Despite acknowledging this fraud mechanism, Chase has not refunded the disputed withdrawals. 

After researching my rights under Regulation E, I sent Chase Bank a written request dated XX/XX/year>, asking Chase to reinvestigate the claim. In that letter, I cited Chases obligations under Regulation E, identified deficiencies in Chase 's investigation, including reliance on PIN use alone, the absence of a reasonable investigation, and the failure to provide written findings or supporting documentation, and requested documentation supporting its determination. Despite my repeated inquiries and requests, both in writing and by telephone, Chase Bank did not respond and did not provide the requested documentation. 

Chase representatives advised that my best option was to contact local law enforcement for assistance with investigation into the matter. I followed that guidance and contacted multiple police departments. The XXXX Police Department agreed to investigate. 

The XXXX Police Department obtained a court-authorized search and seizure warrant requiring Chase to produce ATM surveillance footage. After reviewing Chases own ATM camera footage, the XXXX Police determined that the withdrawals were conducted by multiple third parties who do not match my physical appearance and formally concluded that I am the victim of fraud. 

On XX/XX/year>, I sent a second written letter to Chase enclosing the XXXX Police Department documentation confirming that the disputed withdrawals were unauthorized and criminal, reiterating Chases burden under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, and requesting that the stolen funds be credited and the transactions reversed. I also requested written confirmation that no adverse fraud determination remained on my account. Chase has not resolved the matter and states that its internal investigation is still ongoing. 

I am filing this complaint because Chase denied my claim based solely on PIN use, without conducting a reasonable or good-faith investigation, failed to respond to my multiple written and telephone requests seeking reinvestigation and the documentation supporting its determination as required under Regulation E, failed to identify or escalate an obvious and highly unusual pattern of rapid, repeated ATM withdrawals that fully depleted the account and was entirely inconsistent with my established account history, which consisted of small, routine purchases and no prior ATM withdrawals, and has not credited my account even after ( XXXX ) Chase acknowledged that the withdrawals were conducted using electronically captured card information provisioned to a mobile device and ( XXXX ) law enforcement confirmed, using Chases ATM surveillance footage, that the transactions were conducted by third parties and were unauthorized and criminal.

Reporting a closed account as if it were active, delinquent, or repayment-obligated meets that standard. Discover Bank failed to lawfully correct the reporting once notified, further exacerbating liability. 

In addition to FCRA violations, this conduct may constitute an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice ( UDAP ) under Dodd-Frank Act 1031 due to distorting the consumer credit profile through inaccurate risk signaling and suppressing credit access.

The inaccurate closed-account reporting materially affected lending criteria and distorted risk assessment in violation of federal consumer credit standards.

Issue: Problem with a lender or other company charging your account
Sub-issue: Can't stop withdrawals from your account
Consumer complaint narrative:
This complaint concerns a systemic practice by PayPal , Inc., not an isolated account dispute.

PayPal operates an internal billing authorization token system that extracts funds from consumer accounts after cancellation, refund, and stop-payment notice, without providing consumers or regulators with verifiable records that withdrawals are initiated by merchants or settled to merchants. 

The issue described below affects any consumer subject to PayPals token system.

SYSTEMIC ISSUE SUMMARY PayPal maintains exclusive control over billing authorization tokens used to debit consumer accounts. These tokens : Persist after subscription cancellation, Persist after refunds acknowledging lack of authorization or service, Persist after explicit consumer notice to stop payment, Can not be viewed, revoked, or XXXX by consumers. 

XXXXayPals system allows continued withdrawals without consumer control and without merchant-visible billing artifacts.

OBSERVABLE SYSTEM BEHAVIOR Across affected accounts, PayPal transaction histories display : Debit entries labeled as withdrawals, No invoice records, No subscription records, No contemporaneous merchant billing requests, No settlement or remittance confirmation to merchants.

The only verifiable action is that PayPal debits the consumer account. PayPal does not provide a c
onsumer-accessible audit trail establishing that : A merchant initiated the charge at the time of debit, or Funds were transferred to a merchant rather than retained internally.

REGULATORY IMPLICATIONS ( SYSTEMIC ) This practice implicates multiple provisions of the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E ( 12 CFR Part 1005 ) on a systemic basis, including : Unauthorized electronic fund transfers ( 1005.2 ( m ) ), Failure to honor stop-payment instructions for preauthorized transfers ( 1005.10 ( c ) ), Failure to investigate and correct errors ( 1005.11 ).

PayPals token architecture prevents consumers from exercising statutory rights by design.

CONTROL AND AUTHORITY STRUCTURE PayPal, not merchants and not consumers, controls : Token issuance, Token persistence, Token execution, Token termination.

Consumers can not independently revoke authorization.

Stop-payment notices do not reliably terminate token execution.

Refunds do not permanently revoke tokens.

This places PayPal in the position of effective initiator of the transfer once merchant access is severed.

CONSUMER HARM ( CLASS-WIDE ) The system produces predictable harm : Unauthorized debits after cancellation or refund, Inability to stop payment through ordinary means, Forced card cancellation as a substitute for compliance, Loss of access to funds, Repeated withdrawals without transparent justification.

This harm is structural, not accidental.

REQUESTED CFPB ACTION ( SYSTEMIC ) I respectfully request that the CFPB : Investigate PayPals billing authorization token system as a systemic practice.

Require PayPal to demonstrate, for token-based withdrawals : Merchant-initiated billing requests, Settlement or remittance records to merchants.

Documentation demonstrating the described system behavior can be provided upon request.

Untrained staff may fail to properly verify business ownership, beneficial owners, or identify suspicious activity, potentially violating the Bank Secrecy Act ( BSA ). 

Internal Policy Breaches : Most banks have specific, mandatory training programs and certification processes for employees handling business accounts to ensure consistency and compliance with internal protocols and regulatory requirements. 

Customer Due Diligence ( CDD ) Failures : Proper CDD for businesses is critical to assess risk correctly. A lack of training could lead to improper risk profiling or incomplete documentation. 

Fair Banking Concerns : Incorrect account opening procedures could also lead to inconsistent treatment of business customers, which might raise fair banking practice issues. Which in this case it has.

This position directly contradicts Regulation E.

Regulation E violation : Under 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( 3 ), Chases position that provisional credit may be withheld until a later date ( e.g., the XXXX ) conflates investigation deadlines with provisional credit obligations and is inconsistent with Regulation Es plain language and official commentary. if a financial institution extends its investigation beyond 10 business days, it is required to provide provisional credit within 10 business days for the disputed amount and allow the consumer full use of the funds during the investigation. An institution may not withhold provisional credit for the duration of an extended investigation. Chase has done exactly that. 

I am not disputing Chases right to investigate. I am disputing Chases failure to provide provisional credit during an investigation that has been extended far beyond the regulatory window.

2. That Chase be required to issue immediate provisional credit for the full amount of the unauthorized transactions pending completion of any investigation. 3. That Chase be required to provide a written explanation of its legal basis for withholding provisional credit, including notice of my right to request and receive all documents relied upon in making any determination.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/XXXX, I deposited {$23000.00} in cash into my personal account at Truist Bank. The bank accepted the deposit at the branch, credited the transaction, and issued a deposit receipt, confirming that the funds were received by Truist. This transaction was completed in person and involved cash only, not a check, wire transfer, ACH, or electronic instrument. 

Shortly after the deposit, Truist Bank placed the funds on administrative hold, claiming the deposit was suspected of fraud. I was never provided with any written notice, fraud determination, supporting documentation, or legal explanation justifying this hold. No law enforcement agency contacted me, and I was never informed of any court order, seizure notice, or governmental action involving these funds. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, Truist Bank closed my account while still retaining the {$23000.00}. Despite closing the account, Truist did not issue a cashiers check, refund, or remittance of the remaining balance. I also did not receive any written explanation regarding the continued retention of my money after account closure. 

From XX/XX/XXXX onward, Truist Bank provided no updates, no correspondence, and no resolution regarding my funds. I did not receive periodic notices, status letters, or requests for additional information. For over XXXX year, Truist remained silent while continuing to hold my money. 

When I contacted Truist again after this prolonged period, I was told that the funds were still on hold and that Truist had allegedly contacted another institution that supposedly confirmed the deposit was fraud. This explanation is false, misleading, and illogical, as the transaction in question was a cash deposit, not a negotiable instrument or inter-bank transaction. There is no external institution that can verify or invalidate a cash deposit once accepted by a bank. 

To this day, Truist Bank continues to retain my {$23000.00} without returning it, without providing legally required documentation, and without citing any valid statutory or court-ordered authority. 

IMPROPER CLASSIFICATION OF A CASH DEPOSIT AS FRAUD Truist Banks assertion that a cash deposit was determined to be fraudulent is fundamentally flawed. Cash, by its nature, is not drawn on another institution, does not rely on third-party authorization, and is not subject to return once accepted unless it is proven counterfeit or seized pursuant to lawful authority. 

At no point did Truist : Claim the cash was counterfeit Provide a Secret Service or law enforcement notice Provide a seizure receipt or forfeiture documentation Provide a court order authorizing retention Once Truist accepted the cash deposit and issued a receipt, the funds became a bank liability owed to the depositor, not contingent property subject to indefinite internal review. 

VIOLATIONS OF UCC ARTICLE 4 ( BANK DEPOSITS AND COLLECTIONS ) Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 4, when a bank accepts funds for deposit, it assumes responsibility for proper handling and settlement. Although Article 4 commonly addresses items such as checks, its principles regarding finality of acceptance, accountability, and timely disposition apply here. 

By accepting the cash and crediting the account, Truist completed the transaction. There is no UCC provision permitting a bank to hold deposited funds indefinitely without : Written notice A lawful basis A defined resolution process Truists actions constitute wrongful retention and conversion of funds, as the bank continues to exercise control over money that legally belongs to the depositor. 

VIOLATIONS OF CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION PRINCIPLES Federal consumer protection law requires banks to act in a manner that is : Transparent Fair Timely Supported by documentation Truist violated these principles by : Failing to provide written notice of the hold Closing the account without returning remaining funds Failing to communicate for over XXXX year Providing contradictory and unsupported explanations Under CFPB unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ) standards, it is unfair and abusive for a financial institution to : Retain consumer funds indefinitely Withhold legally required explanations Shift the burden onto the consumer without due process DUE PROCESS AND UNLAWFUL CONVERSION OF FUNDS Truist Banks conduct also violates basic due process principles. If a bank believes funds are connected to unlawful activity, the proper course is to : Notify law enforcement Freeze funds pursuant to a legal hold Provide notice to the customer None of these steps occurred. 

There is no legal authority allowing a private bank to permanently retain customer funds based solely on an internal suspicion, particularly when : No crime has been charged No forfeiture proceeding exists No court order has been issued By continuing to hold my {$23000.00} without lawful authority, Truist is engaging in conversion, defined as the unauthorized assumption and exercise of ownership over property belonging to another. 

ACCOUNT CLOSURE WITHOUT REMITTANCE When Truist closed my account on XX/XX/XXXX, it had a duty to : Return the remaining balance Issue a cashiers check Or provide instructions for remittance Truist did none of these. Closing an account does not extinguish the banks obligation to return customer funds. Retaining the balance after closure, without legal authority, is improper and unlawful. 

FAILURE TO PROVIDE REQUIRED DISCLOSURES AND NOTICES At no time did Truist provide : A fraud determination letter A hold notice explaining duration and legal basis A seizure or forfeiture notice A right-to-appeal or dispute process This lack of disclosure violates basic banking standards and deprives the consumer of the ability to challenge the banks actions. 

ONGOING HARM AND FINANCIAL INJURY As a result of Truist Banks actions, I have suffered : Loss of access to {$23000.00} of my own money Prolonged financial uncertainty Emotional distress Significant time and effort attempting to resolve the issue The harm is ongoing, as the funds remain unlawfully withheld. 

REQUESTED RESOLUTION I am requesting that Truist Bank be required to do XXXX of the following immediately : Release and return the full {$23000.00} without further delay, OR Provide a written explanation, including : The exact legal authority relied upon Any court order or law enforcement directive The date and basis of any alleged fraud determination Absent such documentation, Truist has no lawful right to continue holding my funds. 

CONCLUSION Truist Bank accepted my cash deposit on XX/XX/XXXX, closed my account on XX/XX/XXXX, and has retained my money for over a year without lawful justification. This conduct violates consumer protection principles, UCC banking obligations, and fundamental fairness. 

I respectfully request the CFPBs assistance in compelling Truist Bank to resolve this matter promptly and return my funds.

I am filing this complaint regarding PayPals refusal to provide buyer protection after I was the victim of a confirmed tracking-number fraud / false delivery scam involving an {$730.00} purchase made on XXXX and partially funded through PayPal. 

I purchased a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  on XXXX XXXX Payment was made using a combination of PayPal balance/credits and a linked credit card. The seller provided a USPS tracking number that showed the package as Delivered in my ZIP code. I never received the item. 

Because I suspected fraud, I contacted USPS directly and requested verification of the tracking number. USPS conducted an internal review and confirmed the following facts : The package associated with the tracking number weighed only XXXX ounces The item I purchased weighs over XXXX pound ( XXXX oz ), and with the accessories included in the listing would reasonably exceed XXXX pounds ( XXXX oz ) The package was not delivered to my address nor was addressed to me or my address.

I opened a PayPal dispute for Item Not Received and provided all of the above evidence, including USPS confirmation, package photographs, and explanation of the weight and address discrepancy. Despite this carrier-verified proof, PayPal denied my claim, stating that the seller provided a tracking number showing delivery.

I acted in good faith at all times, maintained a consistent item not received claim, and provided objective carrier verification. PayPals refusal to consider this evidence undermines the purpose of its buyer protection policies and allows a known fraud method to succeed.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint regarding Chimes handling of unauthorized debit card and ATM withdrawals under Regulation E. I reported multiple unauthorized ATM withdrawals totaling approximately {$5900.00}. These withdrawals occurred across different ATM locations, in different cities, over consecutive days, and involved escalating amounts. I have no prior history of ATM withdrawals on this account, and this activity does not match my normal account behavior. 

Chime denied my claim stating that the transactions were consistent with my past activity. This conclusion is inaccurate. Only one small non-ATM transaction was similar to my prior activity, while the ATM withdrawals were entirely inconsistent with my historical usage. I explained to Chime that fraudulent actors commonly mimic small prior transactions to avoid detection, but this explanation was not meaningfully addressed. 

I also reported that my account showed signs of compromise, including logins from unrecognized devices and the use of VPNs. I provided a police report reference number as part of my dispute. Despite this, Chime concluded that no error occurred and closed my claim without identifying any specific evidence that I authorized the ATM withdrawals. 

Chime appears to rely on selective use of behavioral data by citing similarity where convenient while ignoring the absence of any ATM withdrawal history, the geographic dispersion of the transactions, and the rapid escalation in withdrawal amounts. Regulation E does not permit a financial institution to deny a claim simply because a PIN was used or because it can not determine how the fraud occurred.

I am requesting CFPB review of whether Chime conducted a reasonable investigation as required by Regulation E and whether its denial improperly shifted the burden of proof onto me rather than establishing that the transactions were authorized.

RE : Rebuttal to SoFi Bank 's Response for CFPB Case # XXXX Date : XX/XX/XXXX Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau , I am writing to formally rebut SoFi Bank 's response dated XX/XX/XXXX, regarding my complaint ( CFPB Case # XXXX ) concerning an unauthorized {$1200.00} XXXX transaction. XXXX 's response contains demonstrably false statements, continues to misinterpret federal law, and further highlights their ongoing non-compliance with Regulation E.

I urge the CFPB to take further action against SoFi Bank due to these serious and persistent violations. 

SoFi Bank 's False Statements and Misrepresentations : 1. False Claim of Providing Documentation : SoFi states, " ... the documentation used within our investigation was provided to you. '' This is categorically false. SoFi Bank has never provided me with any documentation used in their investigation, in direct violation of 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ). Their previous denial email only summarized findings but provided no underlying documents ( e.g., raw login data, IP logs, device IDs ) nor did it inform me of my right to request such documents.

2. False Claim of Resolution within 10 Business Days : SoFi states, " A provisional credit was not issued as this claim was resolved within ten ( 10 ) business days of you filing the claim. '' This is false and misleading. 
I reported the unauthorized transaction on XX/XX/XXXX. 
Ten ( 10 ) business days from this date would be XX/XX/XXXX. 
Even if an initial denial was issued on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX continued to engage with me, request more evidence, and claim they were filing appeals well beyond XX/XX/XXXX. This demonstrates the claim was not " resolved '' within 10 business days, and SoFi was therefore obligated to provide provisional credit under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ). Their failure to do so is a clear and ongoing violation.

SoFi Bank 's Continued Misinterpretation and Non-Compliance with Regulation E : 1. Misapplication of Regulation E to XXXX Transactions : SoFi 's statement that " XXXX transactions are categorized as cash transactions and therefore, can not be refunded if the transaction was authorized at the time of sale '' is a misstatement of federal law. XXXX transactions are explicitly covered by Regulation E as Electronic Fund Transfers under 12 C.F.R. 1005.2 ( g ). The CFPB has repeatedly affirmed this. The critical factor is whether I authorized the transaction, not how SoFi " categorizes '' XXXX. 

2. Failure to Prove Authorization : SoFi 's core argument hinges on " if the transaction was authorized. '' However, SoFi has failed to provide any evidence that I, XXXX XXXX, authorized this specific {$1200.00} XXXX payment to " XXXX XXXX. '' Their previous denial focused solely on consistent login activity, which does not constitute proof of my authorization under 12 C.F.R. 1005.6 ( b ). I unequivocally state I did not authorize this transaction, do not recognize the recipient, and received no benefit.

3. Continued Violation of Provisional Credit Requirement : As of today, XX/XX/XXXX, it has been XXXX business days since I reported the fraud. SoFi has still not issued a provisional credit, remaining in violation of 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ).

4. Continued Violation of Documentation Requirement : SoFi 's current response falsely claims they provided investigation documentation, and they still have not supplied it, remaining in violation of 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ). 

Conclusion : SoFi Bank 's response is an attempt to evade its responsibilities under federal law through false claims and misinterpretations. Their continued refusal to provide provisional credit, their failure to provide investigation documentation, and their persistent denial of an unauthorized transaction based on flawed reasoning demonstrate a pattern of non-compliance with the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E.

I urge the CFPB to thoroughly investigate these discrepancies and SoFi 's non-compliance, and to compel SoFi Bank to : 1. Immediately provisionally credit my account with the {$1200.00}.

2. Fully refund the unauthorized {$1200.00} transaction.

3. Provide all documentation used in their investigation as required by law.

4. Comply with all other provisions of Regulation E.

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. 
Sincerely, XXXX XXXX

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/year>, Bank of America closed my savings accounts. On XX/XX/year>, the bank issued two cashiers checks for the remaining balances, one in the amount of {$2900.00} and another in the amount of {$7100.00}, and mailed them to my confirmed correct address. I received the {$2900.00} check but never received the {$7100.00} check, despite monitoring my mail closely. I promptly reported the non-receipt to Bank of America and requested assistance. 

Bank of America has acknowledged that the funds are undisputed, that the account is closed, that the check was mailed to the correct address, and that I did not receive it. However, I was informed that the bank will not reissue or replace the missing cashiers check until a full 120-day waiting period has elapsed, regardless of the confirmed delivery failure. During this time, I have been left without access to my own funds, with no interim remedy and no mitigation offered.

While I understand that waiting periods may exist for fraud-prevention purposes, the application of this policy in my case has caused significant and unnecessary consumer harm. The bank is aware that standard mail delivery already failed once, yet has not committed to a safer alternative such as in-branch pickup with identity verification or tracked overnight delivery. As a result, the same risk of loss is likely to recur, while the entire burden of delay and risk is placed on me despite no wrongdoing or negligence on my part.

I am not disputing the banks right to maintain fraud controls, but I believe the refusal to apply those controls in a reasonable and proportional manner is unfair. These are my own funds from a closed account, the obligation to pay is not in question, and safer, verifiable release methods exist. The continued delay has caused financial hardship and leaves me exposed to further risk through no fault of my own. 

I am requesting CFPB review and assistance to ensure that Bank of America takes reasonable steps to mitigate consumer harm, prepares for immediate reissuance once the waiting period expires, and commits to a secure delivery method such as in-branch pickup or tracked overnight delivery rather than standard mail.

Citibank informed me that my remaining balance would be issued by check within 3060 days, but the bank has not provided a clear explanation for the delay, nor a specific issuance date. This prolonged withholding of my funds raises concerns regarding compliance with federal regulations. 

Regulation Violations & Concerns 1. Regulation E 12 CFR 1005.11 & 1005.6 Under Regulation E, financial institutions have an obligation to investigate and resolve account-related issues within specific timeframes and provide timely notice related to account balances and accessible funds. Citibank has not provided sufficient information regarding the status of my funds, nor any documented reason for an extended hold.

2. Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) 12 U.S.C. 5531 Withholding a consumers funds for an extended period without a clear, reasonable, or legally required justification may constitute an unfair practice, especially when the delay causes financial harm or places the consumer in a disadvantaged position.

3. Failure to Provide Required Notice of Adverse Action 12 CFR 1002.9 ( ECOA ) When a bank closes an account, it is required to provide an explanation unless the closure is due to suspected unlawful or fraudulent activity. Citibank has not provided any written reason for closing my account or why the funds require a prolonged review period.

Summary of the Issue Citibank closed my account without providing a written explanation.

I was told my remaining balance would be returned within 3060 days. 
Citibank has not provided : The exact check issuance date The reason for the prolonged review Confirmation of whether funds are held for compliance, fraud review, or internal processing A point of contact who is responsible for the case This delay is causing financial inconvenience and appears inconsistent with federal consumer protection standards regarding timely access to consumer funds.

I am submitting this complaint regarding U.S. Banks handling of a fraud claim involving unauthorized electronic fund transfers, reversal of provisional credit, and improper handling of a compromised account. I believe U.S. Banks actions are inconsistent with the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E. 

On XX/XX/XXXX ( XXXX XXXX ) at approximately XXXXXXXX XXXX., I received a phone call from a number that displayed on my caller ID as U.S. Bank. The caller claimed to be from U.S. Banks fraud department and stated that there may have been fraudulent activity on my account. The caller referenced example transactions and asked me to confirm whether I had authorized them. I clearly stated that I had not authorized those transactions.

The caller then stated that a link would be sent so I could mark the transactions as fraudulent. Because the caller ID displayed U.S. Bank and the caller referenced accurate information related to my account, I reasonably believed the communication was legitimate. I clicked the link, which I later learned allowed unauthorized access to my online banking credentials.

As a direct result of this impersonation and caller ID spoofing, funds were withdrawn from both my checking and savings accounts. These electronic fund transfers were not authorized by me and were the result of fraud.

Later that same afternoon, after initially reporting the fraud, I logged into my account and discovered the funds had already been removed. I immediately contacted U.S. Bank using its official XXXX customer service number. A representative confirmed the activity was fraudulent and instructed me to freeze the account and take steps to prevent further unauthorized transfers. 

On the next business day, I went to a U.S. Bank branch and followed the instructions provided to secure my accounts. I was advised that the compromised account would no longer be used and that a new account would be opened. Based on these representations, I reasonably believed the original account had been closed or permanently restricted. I filed a fraud claim, and U.S. Bank issued provisional credit totaling {$5000.00} in accordance with Regulation E. At that time, I reasonably believed U.S. Bank was conducting a good-faith investigation. 

On or about XX/XX/XXXX, I received a letter stating that U.S. Bank determined the transactions were authorized and that the {$5000.00} provisional credit would be reversed. This conclusion is incorrect and unsupported by the facts. 

At no time did I authorize : The electronic fund transfers Disclosure of my online banking credentials Any transfer of funds to any third party Under Regulation E, a transaction induced by fraud, impersonation, or deception does not constitute an authorized electronic fund transfer. U.S. Banks determination improperly shifts liability to the consumer despite clear evidence of social engineering and impersonation fraud.

Additionally, at the time U.S. Bank reversed the provisional credit, I reasonably believed the compromised account had been closed or permanently restricted based on the banks instructions. Without my clear consent or authorization, U.S. Bank reactivated or otherwise used the compromised account to debit {$5000.00}. This account then became visible again in my mobile banking app.

I subsequently received notice that this account would incur overdraft fees if the funds were unavailable. To avoid additional financial harm caused by U.S. Banks actions, I was forced to deposit {$5000.00} into an account I did not consent to reactivate or reuse.

I have filed an appeal with U.S. Bank requesting a second investigation and have also filed a police report. I have supporting documentation, including screenshots showing the caller ID displaying U.S. Bank, the provisional credit reversal letter, and evidence of the account becoming active again.

U.S. Banks actions appear inconsistent with Regulation Es consumer protections, including requirements related to unauthorized electronic fund transfers, provisional credit, and good-faith investigations. The lack of clarity regarding account status and the debiting of funds without clear consumer consent compounds the harm.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/year>, a XXXX XXXX check in the amount of {$1000.00} was issued by XXXX XXXX to the payee. The check was drawn on a XXXX XXXX account and sent through XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX service. 

On XX/XX/year>, the payee deposited the check into a Capital One account. Capital One received and imaged the check for processing ( the check image provided by XXXX XXXX shows a Capital One XXXX processing stamp, confirming presentment through Capital Ones clearing center ). 

After initial provisional posting, Capital One rejected the check at posting due to a payee name mismatch ( nickname vs. legal name ). Capital One states that the item was not accepted for final settlement and that a return was initiated. Capital One further states that it never received or retained final settlement funds for this item. 

However, XXXX XXXX system shows the check as cleared/paid, and XXXX XXXX states that no return was received. XXXX XXXX therefore has not recredited the drawers account and considers the item finally paid. 

As a result : The payee never received the funds. 
The drawer was never recredited.

The depositary bank states it rejected and returned the item and did not accept settlement. 
The paying bank states final payment occurred and no return exists. 

This creates a failed interbank return reconciliation / misapplied Federal Reserve settlement. Presentment is proven, posting was rejected, and the return did not reconcile. The funds are missing between institutions and are not in either customers account. 

This is an interbank settlement error governed by : Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) Articles 3 and 4 ( including 4-215 and 4-302 ) Regulation CC Federal Reserve Adjustment and Return Rules Under these rules, funds can not disappear, and one of the two institutions must either recredit the drawer or complete an interbank adjustment and credit the payee. 

The requested resolution is : A full Federal Reserve settlement and return trace by both institutions Identification of whether final settlement was accepted or whether a return failed to post Recredit or reissuance of the funds to the drawer pending interbank adjustment Written confirmation of the adjustment and final disposition of the funds. 

The consumer is requesting that the CFPB require both XXXX XXXX and Capital One to perform a formal interbank adjustment investigation, comply with UCC and Regulation CC obligations, and resolve the missing settlement so that the funds are restored to the rightful party.

Despite these clear and significant fraud indicators, the branch teller and branch manager allowed me to withdraw large sums of money without meaningful questioning, escalation, or enhanced verification. The teller even instructed me to re-enter information in response to an automated Citibank email prompt instead of halting the transaction. As a result, on XX/XX/year>, multiple loans were attempted to be opened using my account. I had to call again on XX/XX/year>, to have the entire account properly locked. 2 ) Failure to stop suspicious account activity, despite numerous security alerts, unauthorized access attempts, and a locked debit card.

3 ) Failure of teller and branch management protocols, by approving high-risk withdrawals without appropriate verification or escalation.

4 ) Failure in account closure procedures, allowing continued exploitation even after fraud was reported.

5 ) Delayed and ineffective fraud notification systems, which left me exposed during an active fraud event.

Citibanks expansion of telebanking and digital services carries an increased responsibility to protect consumers and proactively warn them of emerging fraud risks. In my case, critical guidance and protections were either absent or delayed until after the financial harm had already occurred. This failure represents not only a breach of trust, but a serious breakdown in consumer financial protection that warrants regulatory intervention.

After the dispute had been resolved and credited, TD Bank representatives later recharacterized the transaction as a payroll reversal and denied that it was an unauthorized debit. This occurred when I visited a TD Bank branch to request information and records related to the closure of my account. This post-resolution characterization directly contradicted TD Banks written ACH Department determination confirming that the debit was unauthorized, as well as how the transaction originally posted to my account as a direct debit. TD Bank also acknowledged that no authorization or explanatory code was attached to the debit on its end. 

I also requested confirmation of whether my account records were accessed or reviewed by any TD Bank employee or third party outside of routine servicing, including during the dispute review, demarketing decision, or any account restriction period, and whether any internal notes, determinations, or review records exist explaining these actions. My complaint is not about TD Banks contractual right to close an account. FEDERAL LAW Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ) 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq.

CLAIM NUMBER : XXXX I am filing this complaint regarding Bank of Americas handling of a fraud claim involving unauthorized debit card transactions and its refusal to comply with Regulation E requirements, including the issuance of provisional credit.

I timely reported unauthorized electronic fund transfers on my checking account and provided evidence supporting that the transactions were not authorized by me. Bank of America denied the claim and issued a written decision stating that the charge was authorized by you or made by someone who has permission to use the card or account. This conclusion was made without providing any affirmative evidence of authorization, such as a signed receipt, authentication records tied specifically to me, merchant documentation proving authorization, or proof that I granted permission to any third party. 

After I disputed the denial and requested reconsideration, Bank of America reopened the claim. Despite reopening the investigation, Bank of America has refused to issue provisional credit. Multiple representatives and supervisors have stated that because the claim was found not in my favor and later reopened, it is categorically ineligible for provisional credit. I was also told that nobody can help and that no escalation beyond customer service supervisors is available.

This position is legally incorrect and inconsistent with Regulation E. A reopened claim is not final and remains under investigation. Once an investigation is ongoing and authorization is disputed, Regulation E protections apply. Regulation E allows a financial institution to extend an investigation up to 45 days only after provisional credit is issued ; it does not permit a bank to withhold provisional credit in place of it. Bank of America has not identified any specific Regulation E exception that would justify denying provisional credit during a reopened investigation and instead relies on internal policy, which does not override federal law.

Bank of Americas denial and continued refusal to issue provisional credit are based on assumptions and hearsay rather than substantiated findings. Statements suggesting the transactions were authorized because of account history, spending patterns, device matching, or the possibility that someone with permission may have used the account do not establish authorization under Regulation E. The burden of proof rests with the financial institution once authorization is disputed, and Bank of America has failed to meet that burden. Additionally, I did NOT AUTHORIZE these transactions and had a complete ACCOUNT TAKEOVER WITH EVIDENCE!!!!!

Additionally, Bank of America representatives have stated that there are no Regulation E compliance managers available and that only customer service supervisors exist, effectively refusing compliance escalation while continuing to withhold my funds during an active investigation.

As a result of these actions, I have been deprived of access to my funds, experienced financial hardship, and been subjected to an investigation process that does not comply with federal consumer protection law.

I am a visually impaired customer. My wallet, cellphone, and identifying information were stolen, and the thief used the stolen phone and information ( including access to my email and authentication channels ) to take over my Citibank account. The thief then initiated unauthorized electronic transfers into another account using my stolen credentials and information stored in the stolen phone/wallet. I did not authorize, participate in, or benefit from any of these transactions. 

Citibanks actionsinitiating closure, restricting my access to funds, and doing so without providing a meaningful opportunity to be heard or accommodatedhave created severe hardship and raise serious compliance concerns. 



1 ) My Position ( Non-Participation + Identity Theft ) The transactions at issue were unauthorized and resulted from identity theft and account takeover.

i dispute any implication that I engaged in fraud or misuse.

The fraud occurred because my phone and wallet were stolen and my digital access was compromised.

2 ) Consumer Rights & Laws Implicated A ) Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ) and Regulation E ( 12 CFR Part 1005 ) The unauthorized transfers described are electronic fund transfers and are governed by the EFTA/Reg E framework, which provides rights including : The right to dispute unauthorized EFTs and errors and receive a good-faith investigation. 
The right to receive a timely investigation and written results. 
The right to provisional credit in many cases if the institution can not complete its investigation within the required timeframe after notice, subject to the regulations conditions. 
The right to have the bank follow formal error-resolution procedures rather than imposing punitive restrictions on a fraud victim. 

Citibanks approachclosing my account and withholding my funds broadly while unauthorized activity is ongoingappears inconsistent with the spirit and protections of Reg E for victims of account takeover. 

B ) Americans with Disabilities Act ( ADA ) and Disability Access / Non-Discrimination Principles As a visually impaired customer, I am entitled to equal access and non-discriminatory treatment in services offered to the public. When a disability-related barrier existshere, the theft of my phone and identity materials ( which are essential to my accessible banking and communication ) a covered entity must provide reasonable modifications/ accommodations to ensure equal access where required.

Closing my account and restricting funds without an individualized process, without accessible communication options, and without a meaningful opportunity to present my situation and documentation is discriminatory in impact and denies fair access. 

C ) Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) if any negative reporting occurs If Citibank reports information related to these disputed transactions or account closure in a manner that harms my consumer reports or banking records, I dispute the accuracy of any implication of fault. Under the FCRA, furnishers have obligations related to accuracy and investigation of disputes once notified. 

D ) XXXXtate Law / Commercial Rules ( as applicable ) To the extent any transfers are characterized by Citibank as wires or other bank-to-bank transfers, additional legal frameworks may apply ( including state commercial codes and applicable bank transfer rules ). Regardless of classification, the underlying facts remain : these transfers were driven by account takeover using stolen property and compromised credentials. 

XXXX ) Discriminatory Closure + Lack of Due Process Citibank initiated account closure and imposed a long funds hold without giving me a fair chance to speak for myself, provide documentation, or request accommodations suited to my visual impairment. Treating a disabled identity-theft victim as a liability to eliminaterather than a customer to protectconstitutes discriminatory treatment and an unreasonable outcome.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Issue : Debit card dispute improperly denied despite documented proof of counterfeit merchandise I am filing this complaint regarding my banks denial of a debit card dispute involving a charge of {$720.00} for an engagement ring purchased from a business merchant. 

The bank denied my dispute on the basis that the merchant only collected charges for the amount owed for merchandise received. This conclusion is incorrect and reflects a misapplication of federal consumer protection standards. 

The item delivered to me was proven to be counterfeit, and documentation confirming its inauthenticity was provided to the bank. A counterfeit engagement ring is not the item authorized for purchase and constitutes illegal merchandise. Delivery of counterfeit goods does not satisfy delivery of the agreed-upon merchandise and is legally equivalent to non-delivery. 

Under FTC guidance and Regulation Z ( 12 CFR 1026.13 ), a consumer has the right to dispute a transaction when the exact item authorized is not received. Receipt of counterfeit goods constitutes non-delivery of merchandise as agreed, as well as material misrepresentation and failure of consideration. 

Despite being provided with proof that the item was counterfeit, the bank continued to characterize the transaction as valid by asserting that merchandise was received, without addressing the legality or authenticity of the goods delivered. This ignores material facts and improperly shifts liability to the consumer. 

I am requesting that the CFPB require the bank to : XXXX. Reopen and properly reclassify the dispute as non-delivery of authorized merchandise XXXX. Conduct a review by a senior dispute analyst or compliance officer XXXX. Provide a written explanation detailing how counterfeit goods were deemed to satisfy delivery requirements under Regulation Z All supporting documentation proving the item was counterfeit has been retained and is available upon request.

Chase has failed to explain how certain ACH transactions were determined to be fraudulent and reimbursed, while other ACH transactionsinitiated in the same mannerwere deemed authorized without evidence that I affirmatively approved them. Current has not provided any affirmative evidence that I personally authorized these transactions after my phone and wallet were stolen. Statements that the activity did not look fraudulent are insufficient under federal law.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Product : Savings account Company : Wells Fargo Bank , N.A . 

What happened? 

Wells Fargo assessed monthly maintenance fees on my Way2Save savings account despite the account meeting the disclosed minimum balance requirement.

The Wells Fargo mobile app displayed my account balance as {$300.00} as of XX/XX/XXXX, and the balance remained at or above {$300.00} at statement end.

The account disclosure states that the $ XXXX  monthly service fee applies when the balance is less than {$300.00}. The mobile app prominently displays balances to consumers without clearly indicating that those balances may not be used for fee assessment.

Why is this a problem?

This practice is deceptive and unfair to a reasonable consumer.

A reasonable consumer would rely on the balance displayed in Wells Fargos app to determine whether the disclosed {$300.00} minimum balance requirement has been met. 

If Wells Fargo instead uses a different internal metric ( such as a minimum daily balance during the statement period, ledger balance timing, or fee-first posting logic ), that methodology was not clearly or conspicuously disclosed at the time the fees were assessed. 

Charging fees under these circumstances causes avoidable financial harm, requires consumers to spend time disputing charges, and is not reasonably avoidable when the banks own interface presents misleading balance information. 

The fact that Wells Fargo reversed both fees upon contact indicates the charges were improperly applied or inconsistently assessed, reinforcing concerns about systemic misapplication rather than isolated error.

I am concerned this practice may be systemic and affecting other consumers who reasonably rely on app-displayed balances to avoid fees.

Consumer Complaint Narrative Account Closure Following Active Dispute I am submitting this complaint to document the escalation of harm that occurred while my prior complaint was actively under review by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and to explain the circumstances surrounding the formal closure of my SoFi Bank, N.A. accounts in XXXX XXXX 

After discovering a series of unauthorized electronic transactions connected to non-physical, app-based merchants using frequently changing identifiers, I immediately contacted SoFi and repeatedly requested intervention. From the outset, I explained that these were not traditional card-present transactions and asked that the activity be stopped or restricted, including limiting transactions to my physical card only. I was informed that action could not be taken until the transactions fully posted, despite my early warnings that additional withdrawals were imminent. 

Once the transactions posted, I formally disputed them and requested stop-payment protections. SoFi later acknowledged that a stop payment had been entered ; however, this action proved ineffective because the merchants continuously changed their billing identifiers. Each new debit appeared under a different merchant name, allowing withdrawals to continue despite my notice and requests for protection. This structural issue was repeatedly communicated to SoFi, yet meaningful preventative measures were not implemented. 

During the dispute process, SoFi issued a provisional credit. Rather than securing the account after issuing that credit, SoFi allowed the same merchant ecosystem to continue accessing the account. As a result, the provisional funds were withdrawn through newly altered merchant identifiers, creating an overdraft balance of approximately {$6000.00}. This overdraft was not caused by new spending or consumer action but arose directly from SoFis failure to prevent continued debits after fraud had been reported and acknowledged.

While my CFPB complaint remained active, SoFi contacted me by telephone in XXXX XXXX and informed me that my accounts would be closed, citing the overdraft balance created under these circumstances. The closure occurred despite the fact that the overdraft itself stemmed from disputed transactions and from the banks handling of the provisional credit during an ongoing investigation. 

Throughout this process, SoFi repeatedly stated that it had collaborated with merchants and other financial institutions regarding the disputed activity. However, none of the substance of those communications was disclosed to me. I was not provided meaningful information about which entities were contacted, what findings were made, or how those findings justified denying reimbursement. As the consumer directly affected, I was left without transparency into decisions that materially impacted my financial standing. 

The timing of the account closure occurring while a CFPB complaint was pending raises serious concerns. Instead of resolving the dispute or addressing the procedural failures identified in my complaint, SoFi terminated the banking relationship based on consequences created by unresolved disputed transactions. This action compounded the financial harm and deprived me of access to banking services during an active regulatory review. 

This complaint is therefore submitted to address the following concerns : Failure to implement effective protections after timely notice of unauthorized electronic transfers Reliance on stop-payment measures known to be ineffective against merchants using rotating identifiers Issuance of a provisional credit without securing the account against continued withdrawals Creation of a substantial overdraft balance resulting from unresolved disputed activity Lack of transparency regarding alleged collaboration with merchants and financial institutions Closure of accounts during an active CFPB dispute, resulting in additional financial and procedural harm I am seeking regulatory review to determine whether SoFi complied with its obligations under consumer financial protection laws and whether the handling of my disputes and subsequent account closure deprived me of protections afforded to consumers reporting unauthorized electronic transfers. 

I respectfully request a full investigation and a resolution that restores me to the financial position I occupied prior to these events and ensures that similarly situated consumers are not subjected to the same sequence of preventable harms.

I respectfully request that the CFPB review whether Wells Fargos handling of this matter complies with applicable standards governing fraud claim evaluation and whether the banks reliance on authorization alone constitutes an unfair or abusive practice in the context of reported criminal impersonation.

I submit this complaint regarding unauthorized debits, misrepresentation of account status, and potential violations of federal consumer protection statutes by Truist Bank. I. FACTUAL BACKGROUND On XX/XX/year>, I deposited two checks into my personal checking account in the amounts of {$950.00} and {$8900.00}. Prior to completing the transaction, I specifically inquired at the above-referenced branch whether any hold would be placed on the checks. I was expressly assured by a bank representative that no hold would be placed and that the checks would clear the following day. On XX/XX/year>, both checks reflected as cleared and deposited in my account. However, on that same date, Truist debited {$2100.00} from my account without prior notice, written explanation, authorization, or disclosure. When I returned to the branch, I was told this was a back-end office technology issue and directed to contact the fraud department. Upon doing so, I was informed that the debit represented a hold. This explanation is inconsistent with banking practice and account presentation. A traditional hold restricts availability of funds ; it does not remove previously posted funds through a separate debit transaction while allowing the deposited checks to continue reflecting as cleared. The transaction history shows an actual debit, not a standard Regulation CC hold. On XX/XX/year>, the original {$2100.00} debit disappeared from my account. However, it was replaced by a new debit in the amount of {$8900.00} the full amount of one of the deposited checks. I spoke with a supervisor in the fraud department who identified herself as XXXX. During that recorded call : She stated that the {$8900.00} debit was also a hold. She agreed verbally that the transaction appears as a debit rather than a traditional hold. She stated that the hold was scheduled to fall off on XX/XX/year>, but that it had not yet done so. The matter was not resolved during the call. I informed the supervisor that I would be filing a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. At no time have I received : Written notice of an extended hold as required under federal law ; Written notice of suspected fraud ; Written notice of adverse action ; Any documentation authorizing removal of funds ; A consistent explanation from the bank regarding the nature of these transactions. II. LEGAL CONCERNS AND POTENTIAL STATUTORY VIOLATIONS Based on the above conduct, Truist Banks actions may constitute violations of the following federal laws : 1. Expedited Funds Availability Act ( EFAA ) & Regulation CC ( 12 C.F.R. Part 229 ) If these transactions are being characterized as holds, Regulation CC requires : Proper written notice, Specific reason for the hold, Duration of the hold, and Disclosure of when funds will be available. Instead, Truist posted the checks as cleared and then removed funds through debit entries. No written hold notice was provided. The manner in which these funds were restricted appears inconsistent with Regulation CC requirements. 2. Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ) & Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. Part 1005 ) If these debits constitute electronic fund transfers initiated by the bank without my authorization, they may qualify as unauthorized electronic fund transfers. Regulation E requires strict procedural safeguards and investigation requirements before debiting consumer funds under suspicion of fraud. 3. Truth in Savings Act ( TISA ) If Truists deposit agreement does not clearly disclose the authority to reverse cleared funds in this manner, such conduct may violate disclosure requirements governing consumer deposit accounts. 4. Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) 12 U.S.C. 5531 The following conduct may constitute unfair or deceptive practices : Assuring a consumer that no hold would be placed ; Posting funds as cleared ; Removing funds via debit transactions while calling them holds; Providing conflicting explanations between branch personnel and fraud department ; Failing to provide legally required written disclosures. The representation that these are holds while they function as debits may be materially misleading to a reasonable consumer. III. SERIOUS CONCERNS The sequence of : Initial debit of {$2100.00} Removal of that debit Replacement with a debit of {$8900.00} Verbal admission that the transaction appears to be a debit rather than a traditional hold raises serious concerns regarding internal controls, transparency, and compliance with federal banking law. Consumers are entitled to clarity, accurate representations, and lawful procedures when access to deposited funds is restricted. IV. REQUEST FOR RELIEF I respectfully request that the CFPB require Truist Bank to : Immediately restore all improperly debited funds. Provide a written explanation of the legal authority relied upon to debit these funds. Provide copies of all internal records related to these transactions, including fraud flags, adjustment codes, and hold documentation. Confirm whether this action was taken pursuant to Regulation CC, Regulation E, or another statutory authority. Confirm whether this practice affects other consumers. I further request formal investigation into whether Truist is systematically recharacterizing debits as holds in a manner inconsistent with federal consumer protection laws. This complaint is submitted under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge. Respectfully submitted,

Sub-issue: Didn't receive terms that were advertised
Consumer complaint narrative: I previously submitted CFPB Complaint No. XXXX regarding Morgan Stanley Private Banks denial of a promotional cash bonus associated with a Premium Savings Account opened through the E * TRADE platform. Morgan Stanley responded to that complaint, but the response did not address the central disclosure issue and included explanations that appear inconsistent with newly discovered evidence. In light of newly discovered evidence, I am submitting this additional complaint so that the CFPB can review information that appears inconsistent with the companys response. On XX/XX/XXXX, while logged into my authenticated E * TRADE account opened through Morgan Stanley at Work, I was presented within my account dashboard with a promotional offer for a Premium Savings Account that included a promotional code. I followed the instructions displayed in that authenticated interface, entered the promotional code during the account-opening process, and opened the XXXX XXXX Account. The system accepted the promotional code and allowed the account to be opened. The promotional terms displayed during enrollment required that the customer apply the promotional code at account opening, deposit qualifying new funds within 30 days, and maintain the required balance during a XXXX maintenance period. Based on those terms I opened the account and deposited {$100000.00} in net new funds. After account opening, Morgan Stanley confirmed in writing that my account had been enrolled in the promotional offer and later confirmed that I had met the qualifying new money deposit requirement for the cash bonus. After maintaining the required balance for more than XXXX months, Morgan Stanley later notified me that the account did not qualify for the promotional bonus because I was not the original recipient of the promotional email. This eligibility restriction was not disclosed anywhere in the authenticated enrollment interface when the promotional code was accepted and the account was opened. The first time this condition appeared was in communications sent after the account had already been opened and funded. After the original complaint was closed, I located archived versions of Morgan Stanleys own promotional page from XX/XX/XXXX using the Internet Archive ( XXXX XXXX ). These archived pages show that the XXXX XXXX promotion was publicly advertised on the E * TRADE website with a promotional code and an enrollment window extending through XX/XX/XXXX. Importantly, the archived promotional page itself does not state that eligibility is limited to the original recipient of a promotional email. The promotion is presented as a public promotional campaign using a promo code. My account was opened on XX/XX/XXXX, which falls within the enrollment period shown on the archived promotional page. However, in its response to the original complaint Morgan Stanley stated that the promotion had concluded prior to my account opening and that my account was instead opened through a targeted, eligibility-based promotion. These explanations appear inconsistent with the documented facts. The system accepted the promotional code during enrollment and confirmed that the account was enrolled in the promotion. If the promotion had concluded prior to account opening, the code should not have been accepted and the account should not have been enrolled in a promotion. The bank also characterizes the promotion as a public promotional offer while denying the bonus based on a requirement that the account holder be the original recipient of a promotional email. That requirement does not appear anywhere in the promotional page itself. Post-enrollment alerts containing additional disclosure language can not retroactively introduce a material eligibility restriction after a consumer has already accepted the promotional offer and committed funds. I relied on the promotional terms presented during enrollment when deciding to open and fund the account. I deposited {$100000.00} and maintained the required balance during the promotional maintenance period. The funds used to satisfy the promotional deposit requirement remain in the account. Because the archived promotional page from Morgan Stanleys own website does not include the email-recipient eligibility requirement referenced in the banks response, the newly discovered evidence raises questions regarding whether the promotional eligibility conditions were clearly disclosed at the time the account was opened. I am submitting this complaint so that the CFPB can review this additional evidence and determine whether Morgan Stanley Private Banks denial of the promotional bonus is consistent with the promotional offer that was presented during enrollment.

Consumer complaint narrative: On XX/XX/year> at approximately XXXX XXXX, I was the victim of a robbery during which my wallet and mobile phone were stolen. From that time forward, I did not have possession of my debit card or mobile device. At approximately XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/year>, {$4000.00} in debit card transactions were processed from my Chase checking account to XXXX. These were card-not-present debit transactions. I did not authorize these transactions and I do not have a XXXX account. I reported the transactions to Chase promptly after discovering them. Chase denied my fraud claim, stating that Face ID was used to log into my Chase mobile application at approximately XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX. This denial is legally insufficient under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1693 ) and Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005.6 and 1005.11 ). Specifically : 1. Under 12 CFR 1005.6, a consumer is not liable for unauthorized electronic fund transfers unless the financial institution can demonstrate that the transfer was authorized. 2. Under 12 CFR 1005.2 ( m ), an unauthorized electronic fund transfer is defined as a transfer initiated by a person other than the consumer without actual authority and from which the consumer receives no benefit. 3. Under 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ), the institution must conduct a reasonable investigation and determine whether an error occurred. Logging into a mobile banking application does not constitute authorization of debit card transactions to a third-party merchant. Chase has not demonstrated : - That Face ID was used to approve the Robinhood transactions - That I authenticated or authorized the debit card funding - That I benefited from the transactions - That the transactions were initiated by me The alleged Face ID login occurred prior to the robbery time. The unauthorized debit card transactions occurred after my wallet and phone were stolen. Possession of a device by a third party does not equal authorization under Regulation E. Additionally, card-not-present debit transactions do not require Chase mobile app authentication . The transactions only required debit card information ( card number, expiration date, CVV, and ZIP code ), all of which were in my stolen wallet. Chase appears to have relied solely on a mobile login event rather than proving authorization of the debit card transactions themselves. Under Regulation E, the burden of proof rests on the financial institution to demonstrate authorization. Chase has not met that burden. I am requesting that Chase : 1. Reopen the investigation in full compliance with Regulation E. 2. Provide complete transaction authentication records and investigative documentation. 3. Issue reimbursement for the {$4000.00} in unauthorized debit transactions. Chases denial appears inconsistent with federal consumer protection requirements governing unauthorized electronic fund transfers. I am requesting regulatory review of Chases investigation and a corrective resolution. Please refer to the documents I uploaded. This includes Find My on XXXX confirming condition was lost, A screen shot from email thread with XXXX confirming 0 account under association of me, a screenshot showing where card was lost showing which transactions are fraudulent, and finally a screenshot of the XXXX login screen further identifying I have no login ability with them proving I have benefited nothing from these fraudulent transactions.
