They should have been checking my checking account and not other accounts. This was highly confusing because each time they sent me a message about not reimbursing my account, they used a 'different " account name or number and were not checking the hacked checking acct. According to the law, NFCU must reimburse the funds. At the very least, the law says that because my husband and I called NFCU within minutes of the hack, I should only be liable for {$50.00}. But NFCU insists that someone associated with my VISA accoung may have used XXXX to get into my other accounts. This wasn't explained fully to me and every time I tried to get an explanation, NFCU claimed their information was 'propietary ' and they couldn't share it. More and more, it's looking like NFCU is attempting to grasp at straws to find some reason that they can used NOT to reimburse the funds. I never had a XXXX acct, for example. But it was suggested to me by one of the NFCU reps that the whole hack was my fault, that the hacker had my phone number and that phone number was somehow used to access my XXXX card and then transfer funds. But funds from our accounts never changed just prior to the hack. They never changed after the hack with the exception of the missing {$2000.00} from my checking account. In other words, all this nebulous transfer of funds surreptitiously never happened. A straight transaction by someone with this email address : XXXX, sent money straight from my checking account to some company that may be in Florida called XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX. I recited the law to NFCU as I understand it. That is to say, it doesn't matter how the hacker got into my account or through what venue or how he did it, I didn't give authorization for the transfer of that {$2000.00}. Period! And that's what NFCU should be concerned about. Instead, one of their reps grilled me about my computer, how I'd used it, how much time had the computer been on before I turned it off so the hacker couldn't proceed. I told that rep that I had turned the computer off immediatly, within seconds. My husband and I then, as stated, reported the stolen money to NFCU within about 10 minutes. I saw all of this happening. NFCU has closed ranks and continues to refuse to reimburse the money, trying to find any way that they can to make me at fault or somehow connected to approving the transfer of funds to that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX company that I've never heard of. NFCU refused to tell me how/why they came to their conclusions. I have repeatedly told them that they must PROVE that I authorized the tranfer of those funds and they can not because i never approved anything, nor did my husband and we are the only two people who have legal access to our banking accounts. Now, NFCU wants me to return that {$2000.00} by XX/XX/year>, or they're going to take it. I don't have those funds in my accounts. The money... OUR MONEY... was used to pay our mortgage. And the law clearly states under federal banking regulations that the bank should refund our money. They don't want to. And their trying to find any way they can to keep from doing so by implying and the outright stating that I allowed that transfer so it's my fault. I don't know who the hacker was, I have never heard of him/her or the mechanical company and I am NOT going to pay back funds that the law says I don't have to pay. That's like saying that, if you give my your business card with your phone number on it, using NFCU 's logic, you're giving me permission to hack your account by handing over that business card. I explained how hacking works to one rep and how 'RATS ' work ... A Remote Access Trojan ( RAT ) is a type of malicious software ( malware ) designed to provide a threat actor with full, unauthorized, and covert control over a computer or device from a remote location. Unlike traditional viruses that often damage or delete files, a RAT is designed to remain hidden, acting as a " backdoor '' that allows hackers to spy on users and use the compromised machine for illegal activities. NFCU doesn't seem to care that all my infor they 'claim ' the hacker has was obtained through the hacking and that I didn't 'give ' it to the hacker for the purposes of hacking my own account. The fact that NFCU investigated two accounts that had nothing to do with the hacking has me concerned. I am highly skeptical of the lack of professionalism in investigating not only the wrong account numbers, but in their attitude ( speaking of NFCU ) when telling me this is my fault. Consumer complaint narrative: Subject : Retaliatory Account Restrictions After Filing CFPB Complaint To Whom It May Concern, I am submitting this complaint against PenFed Credit Union for what appears to be retaliatory and unfair treatment of my account after I exercised my right to file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. On XX/XX/year>, I filed a complaint with the CFPB regarding PenFeds decision to close my debit card immediately before a holiday weekend without notice. The CFPB confirmed that the complaint was transmitted to PenFed on XX/XX/year>. Since that date fell on a XXXX when corporate offices are typically closed, the earliest the credit union would have reasonably reviewed the complaint would have been the following business days. Prior to the CFPB complaint, my checking account had no restrictions. I had full access to move my funds internally and externally without issue. In fact, on XX/XX/year>, I successfully initiated an external transfer through PenFeds system. I later called the credit union myself to cancel that transfer because I realized I had made an error when entering the amount. At that time, there were no warnings, no restrictions, and no indication that my account privileges would be limited. However, on XX/XX/year>, just days after the CFPB transmitted my complaint to PenFed, I attempted to initiate another external transfer from my account. The system suddenly denied the transfer and instructed me to call customer service. This was the first time I had ever experienced such a restriction on my account. When I contacted PenFed, the representative clearly appeared to be reading from a note placed on my account. The representative told me the reason my transfer ability was blocked was because I previously had a PenFed credit card that had been charged off and sent to collections. The representative specifically stated that the bank has the right to do what it wants. This explanation makes little sense and raises serious concerns about retaliation. That credit card was charged off more than a year ago, yet PenFed never restricted my deposit account during that entire time. In fact, after the credit card was charged off, PenFed continued to allow normal use of my accounts. They even issued me a replacement debit card when my prior card had been compromised. At no point during that entire year did PenFed indicate that my checking account privileges would be limited because of the charged-off credit card. Before the credit card was charged off, I had proactively contacted PenFed and explained that I had lost my job due to circumstances involving federal government employment disruptions. I was making smaller payments while I looked for work. When I obtained a new job, I again contacted PenFed and asked to be placed on a payment plan to catch up on the balance. I was told by PenFed that they could not set up a plan because the account had already been sent to collections, and I was instructed to work directly with the collection agency. During that conversation, I specifically asked whether the charged-off credit card would affect my other PenFed accounts. I was told clearly that it would not affect my other accounts and that PenFed generally does not terminate relationships over a charged-off credit card. Based on that representation, I continued maintaining my deposit relationship with PenFed. Now, more than a year later, and immediately after filing a CFPB complaint regarding the debit card issue, PenFed suddenly claims the charged-off credit card is the justification for restricting my transfer ability. The timing strongly suggests the restriction was not a legitimate risk or fraud control, but rather a reaction to my complaint. Additionally, when I asked about notification regarding these restrictions, I was told that the right to take such action is disclosed in the account agreement. However, my account was opened online, and I never received any disclosure documents electronically or by mail explaining that my account could be restricted without notice. It is deeply concerning that : My account operated normally for over a year after the credit card charge-off. PenFed even issued replacement debit cards and allowed full access during that time. Restrictions only appeared immediately after a CFPB complaint was filed. Customer service representatives referenced internal notes indicating the account had been flagged. This pattern strongly suggests that PenFed may have placed restrictions on my account in retaliation for filing a regulatory complaint. Consumers should be able to exercise their right to file complaints with federal regulators without fear of retaliation or interference with their ability to access their own funds. The timing of PenFeds actions raises significant concerns regarding unfair or retaliatory conduct. Financial institutions supervised by federal regulators are prohibited from engaging in unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ) under the DoddFrank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. In this situation, PenFed allowed my account to function normally for more than a year after the credit card charge-off. The credit union continued to provide debit card services and allowed unrestricted transfers during that entire period. Only after my complaint was transmitted by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau did PenFed suddenly impose restrictions on my ability to transfer my own funds. This sequence of events suggests that the restriction was not driven by risk management or fraud concerns, but instead may have been imposed as a response to my regulatory complaint. Consumers should be able to exercise their right to seek assistance from regulators without fear that their financial institution will retaliate by restricting access to their accounts or limiting their ability to manage their own funds. If PenFed took adverse action against my account because I filed a complaint, such conduct could undermine the consumer protection framework established by federal law and discourage consumers from reporting legitimate concerns. I respectfully request that the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX review whether PenFeds conduct constitutes an unfair or retaliatory practice and whether similar actions may have occurred with other members who filed regulatory complaints. I am also concerned that PenFed may have limited services on my account without complying with the requirements of 12 CFR 701.32, which governs a credit unions ability to limit services to members. This regulation requires that credit unions have legitimate grounds for restricting services and generally provide notice explaining the reason for the limitation. In my case, I was never provided written notice that my transfer privileges would be restricted, nor was any explanation given until I called after the transfer was denied. The explanation provided referenced a credit card charged off more than a year earlier, even though my account had functioned normally during that entire period. The sudden restriction immediately after my CFPB complaint raises concerns that the action may not have been based on legitimate operational or safety reasons. Because this involves blocking your ability to move your own money, regulators may also examine whether PenFed interfered with rights under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, which govern consumer electronic transfers. While banks can block transactions for fraud reasons, they must still act consistently and fairly, and the restriction must have a legitimate basis.

Regulatory and Legal Context I have already filed serious complaints regarding these incidents with multiple federal agencies. I did not authorize any of these transactions, did not provide my account information to any third party, and did not receive any goods or services related to these charges. The transactions show a clear pattern of recurring fraud, including repeated amounts, multiple charges on the same day, and increasing frequency over time. The total unauthorized amount exceeds {$4800.00}. The merchant listed does not appear to be a legitimate business. There is no identifiable website, no customer support contact, and no verifiable merchant presence. This is consistent with fraudulent transaction activity. A full transaction list was provided to Chime and is included with this complaint. I promptly reported the unauthorized activity to Chime, filed Police Report number XXXX, and submitted a formal written dispute. After Chime denied my claim stating that no error occurred, I submitted a written rebuttal requesting reconsideration under Regulation E and asking for provisional credit and documentation supporting their decision. The day after I submitted my dispute, Chime closed my account. This action prevented me from accessing my account, reviewing transactions, monitoring the status of my dispute, and submitting additional evidence. Chime informed me that my remaining funds would be withheld and only released by check after approximately 15 days. This created additional financial hardship and restricted access to my own money while fraudulent charges were still under dispute. Chime denied my dispute without providing evidence, investigation details, or documentation explaining how the transactions were determined to be authorized. Chime failed to conduct a reasonable investigation, failed to provide provisional credit, failed to consider the police report, and failed to provide investigation notes, logs, or merchant validation. Closing my account immediately after submitting a fraud dispute interfered with the dispute process and raises concerns of retaliatory or obstructive behavior. As a result of Chimes actions, I have suffered financial loss exceeding {$4800.00}, loss of account access, delayed access to remaining funds, inability to monitor or participate in the investigation, and significant financial and emotional stress. I am requesting that the CFPB require Chime to reopen and properly investigate my unauthorized transaction dispute under Regulation E, issue full provisional and permanent credit for all unauthorized transactions, provide all documentation used to deny my claim, explain the justification for closing my account immediately after dispute submission, and ensure that consumer funds are not withheld during an active fraud investigation. I am also requesting written confirmation of compliance. Supporting documentation includes the full transaction list, police report, Chime dispute denial, written rebuttal correspondence, and account closure notice.

This complaint concerns two materially altered business checks totaling {$14000.00} that were stolen from the mail, washed, and fraudulently deposited via mobile deposit into personal accounts unrelated to the intended vendor. These items were not properly payable under UCC 4-401. The fraud followed the exact same pattern as four other stolen checks from the same incident, which Chase reimbursed after submission of affidavits. However, these two checks the largest amounts remain unresolved without explanation. My company, XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, reported this fraud to Chase on XX/XX/XXXX, after discovering that two checks mailed to a long-standing vendor had been stolen from the mail, altered ( check washed ), and deposited into accounts belonging to unrelated individuals. The checks involved are : Check # XXXX {$8000.00} Check # XXXX {$6500.00} Both checks were materially altered and deposited via mobile deposit into personal accounts. My business does not write checks to individuals except payroll, and none of my vendors deposit checks via mobile deposit. These transactions were clearly inconsistent with my companys normal payment practices and contained multiple indicators of alteration, including altered payee names and formatting irregularities. Importantly, four other checks stolen and altered in the same fraud incident were reimbursed by Chase after submission of affidavits, confirming the identical pattern of check washing fraud. However, these two checks remain unresolved without a clear explanation from the bank. Under the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC 4-401 ), a bank may charge a customers account only for items that are properly payable. A check that has been materially altered is not properly payable, and banks must exercise ordinary care when processing items for payment. In this case, the bank failed to exercise ordinary care by honoring items with obvious material alterations and mismatched endorsements, and by allowing them to be deposited via mobile deposit into personal accounts inconsistent with the account holders payment history. Additionally, one of the fraudulent checks was deposited into a Chase account, meaning the bank had direct access to the receiving account and the ability to review the suspicious transaction internally. After months of communication, Chase requested signed affidavits, which I promptly submitted. On XX/XX/XXXX, Chase informed me that the affidavits were not on file despite prior submission, and I immediately resubmitted them that same day. Since then, I have sent multiple follow-up requests asking for confirmation of receipt and a timeline for resolution but have received no meaningful response. Because the vendor had not received payment due to these altered checks, my company was forced to reissue the funds, leaving our small business carrying the financial loss while the banks investigation remains unresolved. This situation raises serious concerns regarding whether the bank exercised ordinary care as required under UCC 4-103 before honoring these materially altered items. I am requesting that Chase : Reevaluate the claim under UCC 4-401 regarding altered items that were not properly payable. Provide documentation explaining how the bank determined that ordinary care was exercised before honoring these altered checks. Reimburse the full amount of {$14000.00} so that my company is not left responsible for losses caused by check washing fraud. By honoring materially altered checks that were not properly payable and inconsistent with my account history, the bank failed to exercise ordinary care as required under UCC 4-401 and 4-103. I would also appreciate a written explanation of the procedures used to determine that ordinary care was exercised before these materially altered items were honored.

Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this new complaint against SoFi Bank. They are not taking my complaint seriously and provide ambiguous replies. They acknowledge issuing a stop payment but ignore the changing merchant identity to bypass. They note credits were issued from same merchants for smallest amounts, not justifying how all others are valid though the reversal of smaller amounts from same merchants stands. SoFis response does not resolve the issues raised in my complaint and does not address the procedural failures that led to continued unauthorized withdrawals, the creation of a substantial overdraft, and the closure of my accounts during an active CFPB investigation. The banks letter repeats prior conclusions without addressing the underlying facts, the regulatory obligations at issue, or the deficiencies in its investigation. 1. SoFi did not address the continued unauthorized withdrawals after I provided timely notice My original complaint explained that : I reported unauthorized electronic transfers before many transactions posted. I requested that SoFi restrict activity to my physical card only. I warned that additional withdrawals were imminent due to the merchants use of rotating billing identifiers. XXXXoFis response does not explain : Why no preventative measures were implemented after notice. Why SoFi relied on a stop payment mechanism that is ineffective against rotating merchant descriptors. Why SoFi allowed the same merchant ecosystem to continue debiting the account after disputes were filed. Regulation E requires a financial institution to prevent further unauthorized transfers once the consumer provides notice. SoFis response does not address this obligation. 2. SoFi does not address the overdraft created by its own handling of the provisional credit SoFi issued a {$6000.00} provisional credit on XX/XX/XXXX. Instead of securing the account, SoFi allowed the same merchants to withdraw those provisional funds using newly altered identifiers. When SoFi later revoked the provisional credit, the account reflected an overdraft of approximately {$6000.00}. This overdraft : Was not caused by new spending, Was not caused by consumer action, And arose solely from SoFis failure to prevent continued debits during an active dispute. SoFis letter does not address this sequence of events or explain how the resulting overdraft could be attributed to me. 3. SoFi claims the transactions were authorized but provides no evidence SoFi states that its decisions were based on an analysis confirming the transactions were authorized. However, the bank does not provide : Any authentication data, Any merchant provided evidence, Any explanation of how authorization was determined, Or any details about the coordination it claims occurred with merchants and financial institutions. A bare assertion of authorization does not satisfy the requirement for a reasonable investigation under Regulation XXXX. 4. The merchant information is ambiguous and inconsistent with a legitimate business One of the merchants cited in SoFis denial, XXXX XXXX, lists an address associated with a virtual mailbox service, not a physical business location. This is consistent with high risk digital merchants and fraud linked operations that obscure their identity. This raises several concerns : A merchant using a virtual mailbox can not be reliably verified. SoFi does not explain how it confirmed authorization when the merchants identity is ambiguous. SoFi does not explain how it conducted coordination with a merchant that does not appear to operate from a legitimate physical location. A reasonable investigation requires verification of the merchants identity. SoFis response does not address this issue. 5. SoFi does not address the structural issue of rotating merchant identifiers My complaint explained that the merchants used constantly changing billing descriptors, which allowed them to bypass SoFis stop payment measures. This pattern was repeatedly communicated to SoFi. SoFis response does not acknowledge : The existence of rotating identifiers, The limitations of its stop payment system, Or the banks responsibility to implement alternative protections once notified. This omission is significant because the rotating identifiers were the mechanism that allowed continued unauthorized withdrawals. 6. SoFis explanation for closing my account is unsupported and ignores the timing SoFi closed my accounts on XX/XX/XXXX, while my CFPB complaint was still active. The bank cites a generic clause from its Deposit Account Agreement but does not : Identify which specific provision I allegedly violated, Explain how the supposed violation occurred, Address the fact that the overdraft was created by disputed transactions, Or explain why the account was closed during an active regulatory review. Closing the account under these circumstances compounded the harm and deprived me of access to banking services while the dispute remained unresolved. 7. SoFis response contains factual inconsistencies and omissions Examples include : SoFi claims denial documents were sent on XX/XX/XXXX, which is nearly a year after the events in question and appears to be a clerical error. SoFi references a stop payment request on XX/XX/XXXX but does not address my earlier warnings or the ineffectiveness of stop payment against rotating identifiers. SoFi does not address the lack of transparency regarding its alleged coordination with merchants. These inconsistencies further call into question the completeness of the banks investigation. Conclusion SoFis response does not resolve my complaint because it : Fails to address the continued unauthorized withdrawals after notice, Does not explain the overdraft created by its own handling of the provisional credit, Provides no evidence supporting its claim that the transactions were authorized, Does not address the questionable legitimacy of the merchants involved, Ignores the structural issue of rotating billing identifiers, And does not justify closing my account during an active CFPB investigation. I respectfully request continued CFPB review to determine whether SoFi complied with Regulation E and whether its handling of my disputes, provisional credit, and account closure deprived me of the protections afforded to consumers reporting unauthorized electronic transfers. Signed, XXXX XXXX XXXX

Obstruction of Police Reporting : I attempted to file a police report twice and presented my official FTC Identity Theft Report ( Federal Affidavit ). However, the police refused to open a case without a specific " Bank Affidavit '' from Chase. Chase has refused to provide this document, creating a circular " Catch-22 '' that prevents a criminal investigation and subpoena of the XXXX footage . This circular logic effectively denies my right to a reasonable investigation. Violation of 12 CFR 1005.11 ( d ) ( 2 ) : Chase has refused to provide the " documents they relied upon '' for their denial, including the Device ID, Tokenization logs, and MFA verification history.

Consumer complaint narrative: To the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, I am submitting a complaint regarding Axos Banks disclosure of eligibility requirements for the Axos ONE promotional savings Annual Percentage Yield ( APY ). Axos advertises a promotional savings APY of up to 4.21 % when customers meet certain requirements during a monthly qualification period, including receiving at least {$1500.00} in qualifying direct deposits. The promotional terms define a direct deposit as : An electronic ACH deposit of your paycheck or government benefits. The disclosure also lists certain excluded deposit types such as real-time payments, online banking transfers, ATM deposits, mobile check deposits, and person-to-person payments. However, after my previous complaint was filed, Axos Bank informed me in writing that the bank internally requires ACH deposits to be coded under the SEC code PPD ( Prearranged Payment and Deposit ) in order to qualify as a direct deposit for the promotional APY. Axos stated : Direct deposits received under the PPD ( Prearranged Payment and Deposit ) code are the only ones that qualify for the promotional rate increase. This requirement is not disclosed anywhere in the promotional terms. The promotional disclosure does not mention ACH SEC codes or indicate that eligibility depends on the specific ACH entry classification used by the sending institution. My account transaction records show that Axos Bank itself displays ACH SEC codes within transaction descriptions. For example, my payroll deposits from my employer appear as PPD entries and so was the initial trial deposit on XX/XX/year> from XXXX as payroll administrator for direct deposit set up, while somehow reimbursements processed through XXXX as my employers benefits administrator later appear as WEB entries. These examples demonstrate that Axos determines eligibility based on the ACH SEC code assigned by the sending institution. However, consumers generally can not control or determine how external institutions code ACH entries. Additionally, the promotional disclosure excludes online banking transfers, but the banks internal rule excludes all transactions coded as WEB entries. In the ACH network, WEB entries do not necessarily represent customer-initiated online banking transfers. WEB entries may also be generated automatically by employer payroll systems, benefits administrators, or integrated financial platforms. Because the promotional terms do not disclose the SEC code requirement or explain how Axos determines whether an ACH deposit qualifies as a direct deposit, consumers can not reasonably determine in advance whether their deposits will satisfy the promotional eligibility criteria. This issue also raises a concern under the Truth in Savings Act and Regulation DD, which require that material conditions affecting the advertised APY be clearly and conspicuously disclosed. If eligibility for the promotional APY depends on a specific ACH SEC code classification, that requirement does not appear to be clearly disclosed in the promotional terms. I respectfully request that the CFPB review whether the Axos ONE promotional terms clearly disclose the criteria used by the bank to determine whether an ACH deposit qualifies as a direct deposit for purposes of the promotional APY. Sincerely, XXXX XXXX

Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this follow-up complaint regarding the handling of my prior dispute against Oriental Bank concerning two electronic fund transfers totaling {$230.00} that I reported as unauthorized. In my original complaint, I explained that one transaction in the amount of {$34.00} occurred through an online merchant using what appears to be a misleading and extremely rapid one-click checkout mechanism that processed a charge without any meaningful confirmation step or opportunity to review the transaction details before completion. As a result, the charge was processed even though the transaction was not made with the intention of purchasing the product or service. Immediately after noticing the charge, I contacted the merchant by email requesting cancellation and explaining the accidental nature of the transaction. I subsequently provided the bank with copies of those email communications as evidence of my prompt attempt to resolve the matter with the merchant. Those communications were sent directly to XXXX XXXX ( on XX/XX/year> ) as part of the dispute process. Despite providing the only documentation available to me demonstrating that the transaction was unintended and that I acted promptly to address the issue with the merchant, the bank never acknowledged receipt of this evidence and nevertheless treated the transaction as valid. The second transaction, in the amount of {$200.00}, remains entirely unknown to me and was never authorized. I reported both transactions to the bank immediately and initiated a dispute under the error-resolution procedures established by Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ), which implements the consumer protections provided by the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq. ). Appears that the bank treated both disputed transactions as a single consolidated amount rather than evaluating each transaction independently. Both transactions were resolved under the same determination and causal explanation, which raises concerns that the bank did not conduct a separate or individualized investigation for each amount. The bank initially credited the total combined amount and later reversed it in the same consolidated manner, without providing any documentation or evidence supporting how each transaction was evaluated. This approach suggests that the bank may not have performed a thorough investigation, particularly since I formally requested the documentation and evidence relied upon in the investigation and, to date, nothing has been provided to me. In its previous response to the complaint submitted to the CFPB, Oriental Bank asserted that the account qualified as a new account under Regulation E and therefore the bank was permitted additional time to investigate the dispute pursuant to 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ) ( 3 ). While the bank relied on this explanation regarding regulatory timelines, its subsequent conduct has raised additional concerns regarding its compliance with the procedural safeguards required during the investigation process. During the course of the dispute, the bank issued a provisional credit for the disputed transactions ; however, the bank later reversed that credit and allowed the account balance to become negative while the disputed charges remained posted. The reversal of the provisional credit occurred WITHOUT providing a CLEAR written EXPLANATION of the investigative FINDINGS or IDENTIFYING the factual basis or EVIDENCE relied upon to DETERMINE that the transactions were valid. This sequence of actions appears inconsistent with the banks prior representations regarding the status of the investigation and raises serious concerns regarding whether the investigation required under Regulation E was conducted in a reasonable, thorough, and transparent manner as required under the error-resolution provisions of 12 C.F.R. 1005.11. Additionally, after the provisional credit was reversed, I requested that the bank provide copies of the documentation and evidence relied upon in reaching its determination regarding the disputed electronic fund transfers. To date, the bank has not provided any documentation demonstrating that the transactions were authorized or otherwise valid, including authentication records, merchant verification, card-not-present, authorization data, or any investigative materials supporting its conclusion. The absence of such documentation is particularly concerning given that I had already provided the bank with evidence demonstrating that one of the transactions was unintended and that I had immediately attempted to cancel it with the merchant. Under the error-resolution provisions of Regulation E, when a financial institution determines that no error occurred, the institution must provide the consumer with an explanation of its findings and must provide copies of the documents relied upon in making that determination upon the consumers request ( 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ). Without access to the materials relied upon in the banks investigation, I have no way to understand how the bank concluded that the transactions were valid or whether the dispute was evaluated in accordance with the requirements of federal consumer protection law. Finally, the reversal of the provisional credit caused the account to become overdrawn while the legitimacy of the disputed transactions remained unresolved and while I was actively requesting clarification and documentation from the bank. As a result, I have experienced additional financial harm directly related to the banks handling of this dispute. I intentionally did not re-fund the account during the investigation process because I wanted to preserve the integrity of the dispute and avoid creating confusion about the source of funds or the status of the transactions while the banks review was pending. In fact, during one of my calls with the bank I clearly informed a representative that I would not deposit additional funds into the account until the investigation was completed. Now overdraft! These circumstances raise significant concerns regarding whether the bank conducted the reasonable investigation required under Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ) and whether the bank adequately considered the evidence provided by the consumer during the dispute process. Furthermore, the handling of this dispute raises concerns regarding potentially unfair practices in the administration of consumer account protections under federal law, particularly when a consumer has made a timely report of disputed transactions and has attempted in good faith to provide supporting evidence. Such practices may also implicate the prohibition against unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices under the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 ).

In addition, I work closely with youth in my professional role, and I am increasingly concerned about the rise of scams like this targeting everyday consumers. CFPB Complaint Bank of America , N.A . Company : Bank of America , N.A . Product : Checking or Savings Account Issue : Continued furnishing of materially inaccurate fraud designation in violation of FCRA XXXX ( b ), including failure to review contradictory institutional evidence from the issuing bank during reinvestigation Summary Bank of America has XXXX a Suspected Fraud Activity designation to XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX based on its unilateral classification of a deposited check as altered/fictitious. The issuing bank XXXX XXXX, XXXX. has provided signed, written confirmation on official letterhead that the check was legitimate, personally verified, and involved no fraud of any kind. Bank of America has been presented with this evidence through the formal dispute process and has twice declined to correct or delete the designation. This complaint requests regulatory intervention to compel correction of a demonstrably inaccurate record that has caused approximately XXXX year of concrete banking harm. Factual Background On or around XX/XX/XXXX, I deposited a {$10000.00} check drawn on a XXXX XXXX account into my Bank of America checking account. Bank of America subsequently : Reversed the deposited funds Classified the check as altered/fictitious Designated my account under Suspected Fraud Activity closed the account. Furnished the fraud designation to both XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX At no point was I contacted prior to the fraud classification. No investigation findings were shared with me. No opportunity to provide clarifying information was offered before the designation was furnished. Dispute History First Round of Disputes I filed formal disputes with both XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX challenging the accuracy of the fraud designation. Both agencies notified Bank of America and conducted reinvestigations. In each instance, Bank of America verified the fraud designation as accurate. The reporting remained unchanged. XXXX XXXX Confirmation on XX/XX/XXXX, I obtained a signed, written letter on official XXXX XXXX XXXX from a named, XXXX branch XXXX. The letter states unequivocally that : XXXX. The check was legitimate XXXX. It was personally written, verified, and signed by their account holder XXXX. The account holder was authenticated in person at the branch XXXX. The check was not altered or fictitious in any way XXXX. No fraud occurred in connection with the instrument The letter further states directly : Bank of America reversed the transaction and informed XXXX He that the check was returned under the classification altered/fictitious and treated as suspected fraud. This is incorrect. This is not an ambiguous XXXX attestation. It is a direct, institutional contradiction from the bank on which the check was drawn of the specific factual basis for XXXX XXXX XXXX fraud designation. XXXX Dispute with XXXX The XXXX XXXX letter was submitted as part of a second formal dispute filed with XXXX. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) ( 2 ), XXXX was required to forward all relevant information submitted with the dispute including the XXXX letter to Bank of America as the furnisher. On XX/XX/XXXX XXXX days after the XXXX letter was issued, and after Bank of America received notice of this XXXX dispute along with the supporting documentation Bank of America again verified the fraud designation as accurate and complete. The record remains unchanged as of the date of this complaint. Legal Basis FCRA 1681s-2 ( b ) Duties Upon Notice of Dispute Upon receiving notice of a consumer dispute from a consumer reporting agency, a furnisher is required under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ) ( 1 ) to : ( A ) Conduct an investigation with respect to the disputed information, reviewing all relevant information provided by the consumer reporting agency pursuant to 1681i ( a ) ( 2 ) ; ( B ) Report the results of the investigation to the consumer reporting agency ; ( C ) If the investigation finds the information to be incomplete or inaccurate, report those results to all consumer reporting agencies to which the information was furnished ; and ( D ) If the disputed information is found to be inaccurate or incomplete or can not be verified, modify, delete, or permanently block the reporting of that information. XXXX XXXX XXXX Failure XXXX XXXX XXXX conduct fails the statutory standard on multiple grounds : XXXX. Failure to review all relevant information. The XXXX XXXX letter constitutes the most directly relevant evidence possible a signed institutional confirmation from the issuing bank that the check was legitimate and that XXXX XXXX XXXX classification was incorrect. If Bank of America reviewed this letter and still verified the fraud designation, its investigation was unreasonable. If it did not review the letter, it failed to satisfy 1681s-2 ( b ) ( 1 ) ( A ) entirely. XXXX. No reasonable investigation could sustain this result. The fraud designation rests on a single factual claim : that the deposited check was altered/fictitious. The institution that issued the check has confirmed in writing that it was not. There is no countervailing evidence in the record. A reinvestigation that arrives at the same conclusion without addressing this direct contradiction is not a reinvestigation it is a rubber stamp. XXXX. Pattern of procedural non-engagement. Bank of America has now verified this designation on at least XXXX occasions twice through XXXX and once through XXXX XXXX XXXX without, to my knowledge, ever contacting XXXX XXXX to verify the status of the instrument, requesting clarification from me, or providing any substantive explanation for its continued classification. This pattern is consistent with an automated re-verification process that does not meaningfully engage with submitted evidence, which multiple federal courts have found insufficient under 1681s-2 ( b ). See, e.g., XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX ( XXXX XXXX. XXXX ) ( a furnisher may not simply verify its own records without considering the consumers evidence ). XXXX. Willful noncompliance. Bank of America is a sophisticated institutional furnisher with actual knowledge of its FCRA obligations. Its decision to re-verify a fraud designation after receiving a signed, written contradiction from the issuing bank reflects either a knowing disregard of its statutory duty to review all relevant information, or a reckless indifference to that duty. Either satisfies the standard for willful noncompliance under 15 U.S.C. 1681n. See XXXX XXXX. XXXX of XXXX. XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX ( XXXX ) ( willfulness includes reckless disregard of statutory duty ). Harm The continued furnishing of this inaccurate fraud designation has caused concrete, ongoing harm over approximately XXXX year : -Denial of new bank account applications at multiple financial institutions, directly attributable to the XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX records -Complete loss of access to standard consumer banking services, forcing reliance on alternative and less secure financial arrangements -Reputational damage to my consumer banking profile, with effects that will persist until the record is corrected -Time and financial cost of repeated disputes, evidence gathering, and correspondence none of which has resulted in any substantive engagement from Bank of America Requested Resolution I request that the CFPB compel Bank of America , N.A . to : 1. Conduct a genuine reinvestigation that substantively engages with the written confirmation provided by XXXX XXXX and provides a documented explanation if it continues to disagree with the issuing banks determination XXXX. Complete deletion all fraud-designated reporting furnished to XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and any other consumer reporting agency to which the designation was reported XXXX. Provide written confirmation to me and to each affected consumer reporting agency that the fraud designation has been removed and that the record has been updated to reflect accurate information Documents Attached XXXX. XXXX XXXX written confirmation letter ( XX/XX/XXXX ) XXXX. XXXX reinvestigation result confirming XXXX XXXX XXXX re-verification ( XX/XX/XXXX ) XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX reinvestigation result XXXX. Prior dispute correspondence submitted to Bank of America XXXX. Chronological timeline of full dispute history Closing Bank of America has had multiple opportunities across multiple consumer reporting agencies, over nearly XXXX months to correct a record that the issuing bank has confirmed in writing is inaccurate. It has declined each time. The most recent re-verification occurred after institutional contradictory evidence was submitted through the formal dispute channel that the FCRA specifically requires furnishers to review. This is not a close call. The check was legitimate. The issuing bank has said so in writing. XXXX XXXX XXXX continued reporting of a fraud designation it knows or should know to be inaccurate is a violation of federal law, and it is causing ongoing, measurable harm. I am requesting regulatory intervention because the dispute process the mechanism XXXX created for exactly this situation has failed.

' This written refusal was issued after Huntington had been notified of the dispute and after Huntington confirmed it had reviewed its own account records. Under Taggart v. Lorenzen, 587 U.S. 554 ( 2019 ), a creditor with actual knowledge of a bankruptcy discharge who affirmatively refuses in writing to correct reporting that implies a continuing personal obligation has no fair ground of doubt that its conduct violates the discharge injunction. I am filing this complaint regarding a XXXX transaction that I reported as fraud, which my bank JP Morgan has incorrectly classified as an authorized transaction. The transaction occurred after I was the victim of a social engineering scam in which an individual impersonated a trusted family member and requested money urgently. Shortly after the transaction, I realized that I had been deceived and that the individual was not my family member but an impersonator. I reported the incident promptly, cooperated fully with the banks investigation, and am now requesting a proper review of this claim under Regulation E guidelines. This situation involved impersonation, social engineering, and deception, and I believe the bank has not adequately applied consumer protections designed to address these types of scams. Regulatory guidance and consumer protection principles increasingly recognize that social engineering scams are a common form of fraud and that consumers should be protected when they are manipulated into authorizing transactions under false pretenses. Denying claims solely because the consumer technically initiated the transfer fails to account for the deceptive circumstances under which authorization was obtained.

Consumer complaint narrative: CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION BUREAU FORMAL COMPLAINT Filed Pursuant to 12 U.S.C. 5531 and Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. Part 1005 ) I. PARTIES AND ACCOUNT INFORMATION Complainant : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX Citizens Bank , N.A. Product : Consumer checking account with linked debit card Date of Incident : XX/XX/year> Amount in Dispute : Approximately {$8700.00} ( representing approximately 95 % of the total account balance ) Branch Where Fraud Occurred : Citizens Bank, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX. SUMMARY OF COMPLAINT This complaint is filed against Citizens Bank , N.A. for its failure to comply with the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ), 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq., and its implementing regulation, Regulation E, 12 C.F.R. Part 1005, in connection with its denial of a fraud claim involving unauthorized electronic fund transfers totaling approximately {$8700.00}. On XX/XX/year>, XXXX separate unauthorized transactions were conducted at the Citizens Bank XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX XXXX, XXXX. The complainant did not authorize, conduct, or benefit from any of these transactions. The complainant was at her home at the time of the transactions, caring for her XXXX children, including a newborn. Citizens Bank denied the fraud claim without adequate investigation, in apparent violation of its obligations under Regulation XXXX. XXXX. FACTUAL BACKGROUND A. Account Transfer and Card Issuance The complainants account was transferred to Citizens Bank from a prior institution. Following the transfer, Citizens Bank issued a new debit card linked to the account. This card was intercepted before it was received by the complainant. The complainant never received, activated, or used the card in question. B. The Unauthorized Transactions On XX/XX/year>, XXXX separate fraudulent withdrawals were executed at the Citizens Bank branch located at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX. The combined total of these transactions was approximately {$8700.00}, which represented approximately 95 % of the complainants entire account balance. The complainant was not present at the branch, was not in the vicinity, and had no knowledge of the transactions until after they occurred. XXXX Claim Denial and Lack of Adequate Investigation The complainant promptly reported the unauthorized transactions and filed a fraud claim with Citizens Bank. The bank denied the claim. Upon information and belief, the denial was based solely on the fact that the transactions involved a validly issued card and a correct PINfactors that are insufficient under federal law to establish that the transactions were authorized by the account holder. Citizens Bank failed to provide provisional credit as required under Regulation XXXX and failed to conduct an adequate investigation into the circumstances of the fraud. XXXX Police Report A police report has been filed with the XXXX XXXX Police Department documenting the unauthorized transactions. The report is available upon request. IV. LEGAL BASIS FOR COMPLAINT A. Regulation E Unauthorized Electronic Fund Transfers Under Regulation E, 12 C.F.R. 1005.2 ( m ), an unauthorized electronic fund transfer is a transfer initiated by a person other than the consumer without actual authority to initiate the transfer and from which the consumer receives no benefit. The transactions at issue meet this definition in full : they were initiated by an unknown third party who intercepted the complainants debit card ; the complainant did not authorize the transactions ; and the complainant received no benefit. B. Burden of Proof Rests with the Financial Institution Under 12 C.F.R. 1005.6 ( b ) ( 3 ) and the Official Staff Commentary, the burden is on the financial institution to demonstrate that a transaction was authorized. The mere fact that a valid card and correct PIN were used does not, standing alone, establish authorization. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has consistently held that card present and correct PIN are not sufficient bases to deny a fraud claim. A card that was intercepted in the mail and used by a third party is a textbook case of an unauthorized XXXX, regardless of whether the XXXX was compromised through social engineering, interception, or other means. XXXX Failure to Provide Provisional Credit Under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ), a financial institution that is unable to complete its investigation within XXXX business days must provisionally credit the consumers account for the amount of the alleged error. Upon information and belief, Citizens Bank failed to provide provisional credit within the required timeframe, compounding the financial harm to the complainant and her family. XXXX Failure to Conduct Adequate Investigation Regulation E requires that institutions conduct a reasonable investigation of error claims. An adequate investigation in this case would include, at minimum : review of surveillance footage from the XXXX XXXX branch at the time of the transactions ; analysis of card activation and usage records to confirm the complainant never activated or previously used the card ; comparison of the complainants location data or other evidence establishing she was not present at the branch ; and coordination with law enforcement. Upon information and belief, Citizens Bank failed to undertake these basic investigative steps before denying the claim. V. HARM TO THE CONSUMER The denial of this fraud claim and the loss of approximately {$8700.00} has caused severe financial and emotional harm to the complainant and her family. XXXX XXXX is a mother of XXXX children, including a newborn. The stolen funds represented nearly the entirety of the account balance. The family has endured more than a month of repeated denials and delays from Citizens Bank, during which the financial strain has been acute. The emotional toll of having nearly all available funds stolenand then being told by the bank that the claim is deniedwhile caring for a newborn and XXXX other children can not be overstated. VI. RELIEF REQUESTED The complainant respectfully requests that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau XXXX Citizens Bank to take the following actions : XXXX. XXXX reimbursement of the full {$8700.00} in unauthorized withdrawals, plus any associated fees or charges incurred as a result of the unauthorized transactions. XXXX. Full internal review and reconsideration of the denied fraud claim, conducted in compliance with XXXX XXXX investigation requirements. XXXX. Retrieval and preservation of all surveillance footage from the Citizens Bank XXXX XXXX branch ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, FL ) for the dates and times corresponding to the XXXX unauthorized transactions. XXXX. Full cooperation with law enforcement to identify and apprehend the individual ( XXXX ) responsible for the card interception and unauthorized withdrawals. XXXX. Confirmation of compliance with XXXX XXXX provisional credit and investigation timeline requirements, and an explanation of the basis for the denial. XXXX. XXXX review of Citizens Banks fraud investigation procedures to determine whether the institutions practices constitute a pattern of Regulation XXXX violations. XXXX. ADDITIONAL REGULATORY CONTEXT The complainant notes that this matter XXXX also warrant review by the XXXX XXXX XXXX Comptroller of the Currency ( XXXX ), as the primary federal regulator of Citizens Bank , N.A. The fact pattern described hereincard interception, non-receipt fraud, denial based solely on card-present and PIN-match criteriareflects practices that the CFPB and XXXX have XXXX as XXXX in prior enforcement actions and supervisory guidance. The complainant reserves the right to file parallel complaints with the XXXX and the relevant state banking regulator. Respectfully submitted, ________________________________________ On behalf of XXXX XXXX XXXX : _______________ Attachments ( to be provided upon request ) : Police report filed with XXXX XXXX Police Department ; account statements reflecting the unauthorized transactions ; correspondence with Citizens Bank regarding the denied fraud claim.

On XX/XX/XXXX, funds totaling {$5200.00} were debited from my personal checking account via debit card transactions. My dispute alleges an incorrect electronic fund transfer, because although I authorized payment, the electronic debits were induced by materially incomplete disclosures and resulted in funds being transferred for services materially different from what was represented at the time of authorization. More than XXXX business days passed after I reported the dispute without Capital One issuing provisional credit or completing its investigation. Capital One representatives and a supervisor advised me verbally that the dispute was not eligible for provisional credit because it was classified as goods not as described and therefore not RegulationE. On XX/XX/XXXX, I sent Capital One a written request asking for clarification of how the dispute was classified, whether it was being treated as a RegulationE error, and identification of the specific regulatory basis for denying provisional credit. More than 7 days have passed since that written request, and I have not received a response. During a subsequent call with a Capital One supervisor, I was informed that Capital One could not provide written notice explaining why the dispute was not classified under RegulationE or identifying the regulatory basis for denying provisional credit. Capital One has denied RegulationE protections for a timely consumer debitcard dispute and has refused to document or explain the legal basis for that determination in writing. I believe this reflects a failure to follow RegulationE errorresolution and provisionalcredit requirements and prevents me from understanding or exercising my consumer rights. I am requesting CFPB review of Capital Ones handling of this dispute, including its refusal to apply RegulationE procedures or provide written justification for denying RegulationE classification and provisional credit.

Consumer complaint narrative: I dispute Wells Fargos XX/XX/XXXX response. The banks response is insufficient, conclusory, and does not resolve my complaint. I dispute both the denial of my claim and Wells Fargos refusal to refund the overdraft fees tied to the disputed activity. Wells Fargo says it completed research, but its letter does not show a reasonable, documented investigation of the disputed transfers. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, once a consumer gives timely notice of an alleged error, the financial institution must investigate the alleged error, determine whether an error occurred, and report the results to the consumer within the required time. If the institution can not complete the investigation within 10 business days, it may use provisional credit, but the investigation still must be concluded within the applicable regulatory period, and the consumer must have full use of the provisionally credited funds during the investigation. 15 U.S.C. 1693f ( a ), ( c ). Wells Fargos response does not provide the factual basis necessary to justify denial. The letter says only that Wells Fargo did not identify evidence that the payment was made by an alternate method, could not locate charges on an alternate Wells Fargo account, and found the disputed transactions consistent with prior undisputed activity. Those are generalized conclusions, not a transaction-specific explanation showing what records were reviewed, what merchant or network data was obtained, what account evidence was compared, or how Wells Fargo determined that the disputed transactions were actually authorized by me. Regulation E requires a real investigation and a written explanation of findings if the bank concludes no error occurred. 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ), ( d ). The CFPBs official commentary also makes clear that a financial institution must begin its investigation promptly upon receipt of an oral notice and may not delay until it receives written confirmation. It also states that if an error occurred, the institution must correct the error, including refunding any fees imposed by the institution, where applicable. 12 C.F.R. Part 1005, Official Interpretations to 1005.11 ( c ). I also dispute Wells Fargos apparent effort to rely on prior undisputed activity, receipt of benefit, or a broad transaction pattern instead of proving authorization of the disputed transfers. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, consumer liability for unauthorized electronic fund transfers is limited by law, and the bank must comply with Regulation E before imposing liability on the consumer for an unauthorized EFT claim. 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( a ) ; 12 C.F.R. 1005.6 ( b ) ; Official Interpretations to 1005.11 ( b ). The response is also deficient because it does not provide the documentation underlying Wells Fargos determination. If a financial institution determines that no error occurred, it must provide an explanation of its findings, include notice of the consumers right to request the documents relied upon, and, upon request, promptly provide reproductions of the documents it relied on. 15 U.S.C. 1693f ( d ) ; 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ). The CFPBs official commentary further states that the institution must provide copies in understandable form. I am therefore formally requesting that Wells Fargo produce all documents and data it relied upon in denying my claim and reversing the provisional credit, including but not limited to internal claim notes, transaction logs, account comparisons, merchant information, network records, screenshots, and any other material used to conclude that no error occurred. Regulation E expressly provides that those documents must be produced upon request. I also dispute Wells Fargos refusal to refund the overdraft fees listed in its own response. I had approximately {$30000.00} in a savings account deposited at Wells Fargo with a promotional interest rate which was set to expire on XX/XX/XXXX. Thus, I went home and immediately transferred {$10000.00} from a XXXX XXXX account into my Wells Fargo checking account. On XX/XX/XXXX, I went back into a local branch in XXXXXXXX XXXX to confirm that the {$10000.00} had indeed cleared into my checking account and was available for any transaction. The teller confirmed that this new cash did qualify me for the new, 12 month promotion. To be clear : I was told in person on XX/XX/XXXX, that I had met the requirements for the new promotional rate. Thus, I authorized the immediate transfer of the new {$10000.00} into my savings account. Since this money had already cleared, and was at Wells Fargo, my assumption was that this would qualify me immediately for the new promotion which would start immediately. Thus, I was shocked and disappointed that I actually received 0 interest from XX/XX/XXXX until XXXX. Not only did I not receive any interest on the new {$10000.00} over this time, but my pre-existing savings account with a balance of {$30000.00} was reset from 4 % to 0 % on XX/XX/XXXX despite the fact that I still had an active promotional rate guaranteed until XXXX. The Wells Fargo Promotional Interest Rate Disclosure form states : " The promotional rate will be applied within15 calendar days of meeting the balance requirement. '' Thus, Wells Fargo 's contention is that they have met their contractual obligations and can refuse to pay any of the interest. My opinion, however, is that the contract wording is intentionally deceptive. A reasonable lay person reading this contract language would assume that if there is a hold it will because of a legitimate purpose -- for example, time needed to insure that the new money requirement has been satisfied. If the bank 's intension is to hold ALL new deposits without interest for 15 days then it should specify this in plain English. My understanding on XX/XX/XXXX was that my new cash had cleared into my bank account and that I was thus qualified to receive the promotion immediately ( that was, after all, the whole reason that I made two in person trips to the bank ). If this was not the case, I think it should have been incumbent on the bank teller to inform me that I would receive NO interest on the {$10000.00} for 15 days. He should also have been obligated to inform me that by signing a new contract that I would also lose all the interest on the {$30000.00} from XXXX. Interest that I was already entitled to by my old contract. Had I known these facts, I would never have agreed to the terms. I would have put the minimum ( {$10000.00} ) in a new Wells Savings account and then transferred the {$30000.00} back into my XXXX XXXX XXXX to prevent losing the 15 days worth of interest on this cash. I believe the contract ambiguity and the lack of any clear explanation by multiple bank tellers is an intentional practice by Wells Fargo so that they can hold funds without paying interest for extended periods. In the modern world, there are very rarely any legitimate reasons why a funds hold of 15 days should be needed. This practice is deceptive and unethical. And when extended over millions of accounts, it also is making the bank an enormous amount of money.

Additionally, under the NACHA Operating Rules, an ACH debit must be consistent with the authorization provided by the consumer, including the identity of the receiving party. A transaction that is processed to a dierent recipient than the one authorized does not comply with those requirements. This transaction was also made under materially misleading conditions. Subsequent ocial communications from XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX confirmed serious financial irregularities, including misrepresentation of financial condition, undisclosed debt, and ongoing investigation into the conduct of its executive director. Independent reporting and legal filings further corroborate fraudulent conduct. The school has also been unable to confirm the location or availability of prepaid tuition funds. Without provisional credit, the investigation should have been completed within 10 business days. No request for information, evidence, receipts, correspondence, or any other supporting material was made at any point during the first 89 days. Although the merchant provided a tracking number indicating delivery on XX/XX/XXXX, the item was never received at the delivery location.A formal dispute was initiated with the financial institution after several failed attempts to resolve the issue directly with the merchant. Specifically, on XX/XX/XXXX, a customer care escalation was sent to the third-party seller stating that a refund " needs to be sent to the customer 's original payment method '' and that the merchant might " proactively refund the customer '' if the seller did not respond within 48 hours. On XX/XX/XXXX, a merchant representative confirmed during a recorded call that a refund request had been submitted and should be received within 48 hours.This complaint is filed under Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005.11 ) regarding a billing error. The financial institution has failed to conduct a reasonable investigation by ignoring the merchants documented admission that a refund is due. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, the failure to honor a promised credit constitutes a billing error that the bank is obligated to correct. I am requesting a permanent restoration of the {$96.00} to my account based on the merchants own evidence of an unfulfilled refund promise.FORMAL REBUTTAL & STATEMENT OF FACT TO : Capital One XXXX Department Regarding Claim : XXXX for $ XXXXMerchant : Walmart XXXX XXXX Dispute Type : Credit Promised but Not Received / Goods Not Received I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT I am formally requesting a reinvestigation of the aforementioned claim. The previous denial was based on a tracking number provided by the merchant. However, the merchants own internal records ( provided in the claim documents ) and recorded transcripts of our communications prove that the merchant admitted the delivery failed, admitted the seller was at fault, and explicitly promised a refund that was never issued.The merchant is attempting to engage in a " liability loop '' where Walmart points to the third-party seller, the seller points to the carrier ( XXXX ), and the carrier points to a GPS scanwhile ignoring the fact that the Merchant of Record ( Walmart ) has already legally admitted fault. II. REBUTTAL OF MERCHANT EVIDENCE. The evidence provided by the merchant is legally insufficient to deny this claim for the following reasons : Failure of Proof of Possession : The XXXX log provided by the merchant shows a " Front Door '' scan. Under UCC 2-509, the risk of loss in a consumer contract remains with the seller until the goods are duly tendered to the buyer. A tracking scan is not " Proof of Possession ''. No photo or signature was provided to prove that I ever received the item.Internal Admission of Liability : On Page 11 of the merchants own evidence PDF, Walmarts internal escalation team states : " ... a refund needs to be sent to the customer 's original payment method... If there has been no reply... Walmart may proactively refund the customer ''. This proves that Walmarts internal investigation already determined I was owed a refund, contradicting the defense they provided to Capital One.The Sellers Conditional Promise : On Page 10 of the evidence PDF, the seller ( XXXX ) states : " ... if they are unable to locate it [ the package ], a full refund will be issued ''. The package was never located ; therefore, the merchant is contractually bound by their own written policy to issue the refund.III. EVIDENCE OF PROMISED CREDIT ( TRANSCRIPT DATA ) I am submitting a transcript of a call with Walmart, where the agent states : " I submitted the request for you to get a refund, and you should receive an email regarding the refund within 48 hours ''. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( Regulation E ), a " billing error '' includes the merchant 's failure to properly credit a return to the consumer 's account. Because the merchant promised a credit to resolve a failed delivery and then failed to issue that credit, a billing error has occurred. IV. APPLICABLE LAW : Ohio Consumer Sales Practices Act ( CSPA ) : Under Ohio law, it is an unfair and deceptive act for a supplier to represent that a refund will be provided and then fail to provide it.Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) 2-509 : The merchant bears the risk of loss for goods in transit until they are actually received by the consumer. A mere " delivered '' scan does not shift the risk of loss to the consumer if the consumer asserts non-receipt.Promissory Estoppel : The merchant made an unambiguous promise of a refund. I relied on that promise to my detriment, and the merchant is legally barred from rescinding that promise.V. CONCLUSION The merchant is attempting to " kick the can down the road '' by citing a tracking number that their own internal team has already deemed insufficient for a successful delivery. Since the merchant has admitted in writing and verbally that I am owed a refund, I request that Capital One honor the merchants own admission of liability and reverse the charge.Declaration : I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true and correct.Signed : XXXX Date : XX/XX/XXXX XXXX

Consumer complaint narrative: I am filing this complaint against Current Bank regarding their handling of my dispute over unauthorized charges totaling {$1000.00} from XXXX XXXX XXXX that were taken from my account without my knowledge or consent. I authorized only a single {$12.00} XXXX ride. What follows is a detailed account of every step I have taken and every failure by Current Bank to properly investigate my claim. What happened : On XX/XX/year>, XXXX separate charges from " XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX '' totaling {$1000.00} were debited from my Current Bank account when I only authorized a single {$12.00} ride. I had no prior knowledge of these rental fees, and was never informed of the amounts that would be debited at the time of trying to pay for only the single ride, and did not consent to these charges. I contacted XXXX immediately upon discovering the charges. A XXXX representative told me I would receive a follow-up email. I never received that email. I followed up with Lyft in writing and received only a response of " warm regards '' with no resolution, no explanation, and no refund. Current Bank 's investigation failure : I filed a dispute with Current Bank promptly after the charges appeared. Current denied my dispute in less than XXXX business day, far short of the XXXX business day investigation period required under Regulation E. No provisional credit was issued at any point during this process. Current Bank also applied the wrong legal standard. When I requested the documentation used to deny my dispute, Current provided the following explanation : " The disputed transaction did not reflect indicators of unauthorized use or account compromise. The review showed that the phone associated with the account was in the cardholder 's possession, and the transaction was tokenized on a known device. There was no new login activity or decline activity, and prior merchant history was present. '' This response demonstrates that Current investigated my claim as a fraud or identity theft dispute rather than as a billing error claim, which is what I actually filed. I never claimed my account was compromised or that someone stole my card. My claim is that a merchant charged me amounts I never authorized or agreed to which is a billing error under Regulation E, not a fraud claim. The fact that my phone was in my possession and the transaction occurred on a known device is completely irrelevant to whether the merchant had authorization to charge me {$1000.00} in rental fees at that time I had no prior knowledge of. Current applied entirely the wrong investigation criteria to my dispute. Current Bank refused to process my appeal. After I attempted to file a formal appeal and submitted a police report as supporting evidence, Current refused to process the appeal on the grounds that the police report had not yet been assigned an official case number only a tracking number. A police report tracking number confirming a report was filed is legitimate supporting documentation. Furthermore, Regulation E does not require a police report as a prerequisite for investigating or appealing a billing error dispute. Current 's refusal to process my appeal on this basis is an additional violation of my rights under federal law. The following are steps I have taken : Contacted Lyft immediately and received no resolution Filed a dispute with Current Bank promptly Requested and received Current 's investigation findings in writing Filed a police report documenting the unauthorized charges Attempted to file a formal appeal which Current refused to process Contacted my U.S. Senator 's office for constituent assistance
