Consumer complaint narrative: XX/XX/XXXX Consumer Financial Protection Bureau XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX Washington , DC XXXX ( Submission contemplated via consumerfinance.gov/complaint with this letter and the enclosures attached as supporting documents. ) Re : Complaint Against U.S. Bank National Association Inadequate Investigation, Inadequate Customer Communication, and Failure to Reimburse {$53000.00} in Unauthorized ACH Transactions ( Account ending in XXXX ) Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( formerly XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) ( XXXX ), an Arkansas business, submits this complaint against U.S. Bank National Association ( U.S. Bank ). XXXX account is a commercial deposit account, and XXXX acknowledges that some of the consumer-protection statutes and regulations the Bureau ordinarily enforces including Regulation E do not apply to commercial accounts. XXXX nonetheless brings this complaint to the Bureau because the conduct described below an inadequate fraud investigation, an unsubstantiated denial of reimbursement, a closing communication that contained no findings, and a formal response that mischaracterizes the customers contact implicates U.S. Banks customer-communications and dispute-handling practices generally, and because the Bureaus public complaint database serves an important function in documenting patterns of conduct by federally regulated financial institutions. Complainant and Subject Institution Complainant : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( formerly XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) Address : XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX Authorized representative : XXXX XXXX, XXXX ( XXXX ) Subject institution : U.S. Bank National Association Account : U.S. Bank commercial deposit account ending in XXXX, accessed through the U.S. Bank XXXX ( commercial online banking ) platform. Summary of the Complaint On XX/XX/XXXX, an impersonator obtained XXXX XXXX credentials by means of a phishing telephone call that displayed a U.S. Bank-branded caller-ID and email communications sent from XXXX, U.S. Banks legitimate SinglePoint customer-service email address. XXXX XXXX promptly notified U.S. Bank by email and telephone the same day. On the XXXX Customer Service call, U.S. Bank told XXXX the Account had been flagged with the Fraud Department and that all transactions would be reviewed before execution. Approximately twenty hours later, U.S. Bank executed three of four unauthorized ACH payment orders that had been submitted by the impersonator using the compromised credentials, diverting {$53000.00}. U.S. Bank closed its case on XX/XX/XXXX without findings, by way of a brief email from a local-branch employee that itself acknowledged the open question of what actions took place concerning the fraud conversation on XX/XX/XXXX with customer service. U.S. Banks formal response of XX/XX/XXXX from the banks XXXX XXXX XXXX, signed by XXXX XXXX declined reimbursement, characterized XXXX XX/XX/XXXX notice as merely an access issue, and pointed XXXX to the Security provisions of the Deposit Account Agreement. The response did not address or even acknowledge the central facts : the 20-hour notice window, the verbal assurance from the banks representative, and the banks execution of the orders despite that assurance. Chronology of Events On the morning of XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX, an Accounts Payable employee of XXXX, received a telephone call. The caller-ID displayed U.S. Bank as the source of the call. The caller represented himself or herself to be a U.S. Bank employee, told XXXX XXXX that XXXX account had been the subject of fraudulent activity, and asked for login information to address the situation. During the call the caller also sent XXXX XXXX PIN-related emails purporting to come from XXXX the U.S. Bank XXXX customer-service email address. Believing the call to be legitimate, XXXX XXXX provided XXXX XXXX login credentials. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, emailed XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX U.S. Bank personnel known to her at U.S. Banks XXXX branches to alert U.S. Bank to the suspicious activity. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX also called U.S. Banks XXXX Customer Service line at XXXX. During that call, the U.S. Bank representative confirmed that the earlier call received by XXXX XXXX was an impersonator and informed XXXX XXXX that the U.S. Bank Fraud Department had flagged XXXX account and would review all of XXXX transactions before execution. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, during the same call, the U.S. Bank representative emailed XXXX XXXX instructions to change XXXX password. XXXX XXXX did so immediately. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX four minutes after XXXX XXXX call to XXXX XXXX XXXX began an unauthorized actor used the previously-obtained XXXX credentials to submit four ACH payment orders totaling {$68000.00} against XXXX account . The orders were not scheduled to execute that day ; they were scheduled for execution the following business day, XX/XX/XXXX. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX of the local U.S. Bank branch responded to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX email, instructing her to call the XXXX Customer Service number a step XXXX XXXX had already independently taken six minutes earlier. At XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX received written confirmation from U.S. Bank that XXXX account credentials had been reset. As of this point in the timeline, U.S. Bank had : ( i ) been notified by email of the suspicious activity, ( ii ) been notified by telephone of the suspicious activity, ( iii ) confirmed by telephone that the originating call was an impersonator, ( iv ) represented that the Fraud Department had flagged the account and would review all transactions before execution, and ( v ) reset XXXX account credentials. The four unauthorized payment orders sat in the banks queue overnight, scheduled for execution the next business day. Notwithstanding all of the foregoing, on the morning of XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank executed three of the four unauthorized payment orders, resulting in the diversion of {$53000.00} from XXXX account. The fourth order, in the amount of {$15000.00} payable to XXXX XXXX, was not completed because the receiving account had been closed. XXXX XXXX was monitoring the account on the morning of XX/XX/XXXX and saw the executions as they posted. At approximately XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, she contacted U.S. Bank to report the unauthorized executions. U.S. Bank assigned ticket number XXXX and instructed her to wait for a call from the Fraud Department . No such call was received. At approximately XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX called U.S. Bank again and spoke with XXXX XXXX, who informed her for the first time that XXXX needed to submit an ACH Service Request Adjustment Form. XXXX XXXX completed and submitted the form the same day. Approximately one hour later, U.S. Bank confirmed by email that the {$15000.00} transfer to XXXX XXXX had not gone through because the receiving account had been closed ; the bank stated it was attempting to retrieve the remaining funds from the receiving banks. From XX/XX/XXXX forward, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX ( then XXXX Chief Executive Officer ; XXXX XXXX transitioned to a consultant role effective XX/XX/XXXX, at which time XXXX XXXX became President of the company ) contacted U.S. Bank on at least ten occasions seeking information on the recovery effort and reimbursement of the diverted funds. At XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX XXXX of the local U.S. Bank branch emailed XXXX XXXX to inform XXXX that U.S. Bank had been unable to recover the diverted funds. XXXX XXXX email stated : the ACH fraud department has closed the case. In the same email, XXXX XXXX also wrote : So, I guess the question is what actions took place concerning the fraud conversation on XX/XX/XXXX with customer service. That sentence from a U.S. Bank employee reflects the central unanswered question that frames this complaint. On XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX sent U.S. Bank a formal demand letter via certified mail and email, addressed to the Vice President of the XXXX Branch, the XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the General Counsel. The letter set out the chronology, demanded reimbursement of {$53000.00} within fourteen days, and put U.S. Bank on notice to preserve all related documents and communications. On XX/XX/XXXX, U.S. Bank responded by letter signed by XXXX XXXX, Senior Vice President and Head of Enterprise Complaints. The response declined reimbursement, characterized XXXX XXXX XX/XX/XXXX contact as merely an access issue, categorized the loss as an account takeover, and pointed XXXX to the Security provisions of the Deposit Account Agreement. The response did not address or even acknowledge ( i ) the approximately 20-hour notice period before the unauthorized executions, ( ii ) the bank representatives confirmation that the account had been flagged and would be subject to transaction review, or ( iii ) the banks execution of the orders despite that representation. Note on the recovery facts : U.S. Banks XX/XX/XXXX letter states that one transaction in the amount of {$15000.00} was successfully reversed and credited. XXXX contemporaneous record reflected both in U.S. Banks own emails to XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX and in XXXX XX/XX/XXXX letter is that this transaction was never completed because the receiving bank account had been closed. The accounts of why {$15000.00} was not lost differ ; the operative fact for purposes of this complaint is that {$53000.00} remains unreimbursed. Bureau-Relevant Aspects of the Complaint Smiths respectfully draws the Bureaus attention to the following aspects of U.S. Banks conduct that bear on the Bureaus general supervisory interest in consumer-facing communications and dispute-handling practices, even though the underlying account is commercial : ( a ) Inadequate investigation findings communicated to the customer. U.S. Banks XX/XX/XXXX closure communication contained no findings, no description of the banks investigative steps, and no explanation of the banks decision even as the banks own employee acknowledged in that communication that the relationship between the customers XX/XX/XXXX notice and the banks subsequent execution of the orders was an unanswered question. ( b ) Mischaracterization of the customers notice in the formal response. The banks XX/XX/XXXX response describes XXXX XX/XX/XXXX contact as merely an access issue, which is inconsistent with the banks own contemporaneous conduct of flagging the account with the Fraud Department. Banks do not flag access issues with their fraud departments. The mischaracterization is the kind of dispute-response framing that the Bureaus complaint database is well-suited to document. ( c ) Use of the banks own customer-facing communications channels in the fraud. The fraud was effected through the impersonation of U.S. Banks caller-ID and the use of XXXX ( an actual U.S. Bank customer-service address ) to send PIN-related material to the customer. The Bureaus scrutiny of bank communications practices is well-served by examining whether U.S. Bank has adequate controls over the impersonation of its own outbound channels. ( d ) Public-database documentation. Even if the Bureau ultimately concludes that direct intervention is not appropriate for this commercial-account dispute, the Bureaus public complaint database serves an important function in documenting institutional conduct. XXXX respectfully requests that this complaint be accepted and made available in the database to that end. Resolution Requested XXXX XXXX XXXX respectfully requests that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau consider the following actions : ( a ) Open a formal complaint matter with U.S. Bank and require the bank to provide a written response that addresses the specific factual allegations summarized above, including the 20-hour notice window, the verbal assurance regarding transaction review , and the basis for executing the payment orders after the account had been flagged. ( b ) Request, as part of the agencys review, that U.S. Bank produce or preserve ( i ) the audio recording and any transcript of the XXXX XXXX CST on XX/XX/XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX call, ( ii ) internal records reflecting the flagging of XXXX account by the Fraud Department, and ( iii ) records reflecting why the four unauthorized payment orders were executed despite the flag. ( c ) Facilitate a review of U.S. Banks reimbursement decision so that, on the merits and on a complete record, the bank may reconsider its denial of reimbursement of the {$53000.00} diverted from XXXX account. Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this complaint against JPMorgan Chase Bank , N.A . / Chase Bank regarding a foreign currency exchange transaction debited from my Chase checking account ending in XXXX. I initiated the currency exchange transaction on XX/XX/year>, and picked up the XXXX pesos on XX/XX/year>, at the Chase branch located at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXXXXXX. Chase debited {$990.00} USD from my checking account ending in XXXX and provided XXXX XXXX pesos ( XXXX ). Chase used an exchange rate of XXXX USD per XXXX. Before going to Chase, I looked online and understood that Chases foreign currency exchange cost or commission may be approximately 3 % to 5 %. I was willing to proceed based on that general range. I was not willing to proceed with an exchange-rate cost approaching 9.91 % to 10 %, and that level of cost was not clearly disclosed to me before the transaction. The market/reference rate I found for the same general period was approximately XXXX USD per XXXX. Using that benchmark, {$990.00} USD should have produced approximately XXXX XXXX, not XXXX XXXX. The difference is approximately XXXX XXXX. Item Calculation Result Chase rate XXXX USD per XXXX XXXX XXXX USD XXXXXXXX XXXX Market/reference rate XXXX USD per XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Chase markup vs. reference rate ( XXXX XXXX ) XXXX 9.91 % higher XXXX expected at market rate {$990.00} XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX Chase provided {$990.00} XXXX about XXXXXXXX XXXX Difference XXXX XXXX approximately XXXXXXXX XXXX less Before completing or accepting the transaction, I specifically asked Chase representatives whether there were any fees. I asked because the receipt did not clearly disclose any actual fee, commission, spread, vendor markup, or embedded exchange-rate cost. I was told there were no fees. However, the receipt states that Chases foreign exchange rates include spreads paid to Chase and its vendors and that Chase may make a commission for providing foreign exchange services. Had Chase clearly disclosed before the transaction that the exchange rate included an embedded spread, commission, vendor markup, or other cost approaching 9.91 % to 10 %, I would not have completed the transaction with Chase. I relied on the statement that there were no fees, and I was not provided a clear, upfront disclosure showing the actual cost built into the exchange rate. After I discovered the exchange-rate issue, I attempted to have Chase reverse or unwind the transaction. Chase refused. The branch manager stated that there was nothing she could do. Instead of reversing the transaction at the original rate, Chase offered to buy back the same XXXX pesos at a worse exchange rate of XXXX USD per XXXX. Item Calculation Amount Original amount debited from checking {$990.00} Chase buy-back offer XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX {$810.00} Total loss if I accepted buy-back {$990.00} {$810.00} {$180.00} This placed me in a forced-loss position. Chase refused to unwind the transaction after I raised the disclosure issue, and the only alternative Chase offered would have caused me to lose approximately {$180.00} in total. Because I am leaving for my vacation and must use the XXXX pesos, I no longer have a practical option to return the currency. The branch manager also stated, in substance, that as long as she has been working for Chase, no one has ever complained about the foreign currency exchange disclosures. That statement reinforced my concern that this may be a systemic issue, not merely a one-time misunderstanding. It suggests that Chase branch management and staff may not be properly trained on Chases disclosure obligations or may not understand the compliance risks involved when customers are told there are no fees while Chase may still earn compensation through an embedded spread, commission, vendor payment, or exchange-rate adjustment. The absence of prior customer complaints does not mean the disclosure was adequate or legally compliant. It may instead indicate that customers were not aware of the embedded cost or did not understand that the exchange rate included compensation to Chase or its vendors. This is precisely why clear, upfront disclosure is necessary. I believe Chases conduct was unfair and deceptive. Chases representative told me there were no fees, but Chases receipt indicates that Chase may receive compensation through spreads, vendor payments, and/or commissions. Whether Chase labels the cost as a fee, spread, commission, vendor markup, or exchange-rate adjustment, the practical result was the same : Chase used a materially worse exchange rate and did not clearly disclose the embedded cost before debiting my checking account. This conduct appears to implicate federal consumer financial protection laws and regulations, including the following : Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ). The CFPB states that under the Dodd-Frank Act, it is unlawful for providers of consumer financial products or services to engage in unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices. Chases statement that there were no fees, combined with an undisclosed embedded exchange-rate cost approaching 10 %, raises deceptive and unfair-practice concerns. Its deceptive because Chase did not properly disclose the fees, and tow representative stated there are no fees. It is unfair because as a consumer, once they took the money out of my account, I had no recourse for them to correct the mistake of insufficient disclosure and the charged my {$97.00}. Regulation E / Electronic Fund Transfer Act. Because the funds were debited directly from my Chase checking account, this also raises transaction-disclosure and error-resolution concerns. Regulation E applies to electronic fund transfers that authorize a financial institution to debit or credit a consumers account. Chase should explain whether this checking-account debit was treated as an electronic fund transfer and, if so, what disclosures and error-resolution rights applied. Truth in Savings Act / Regulation DD. Regulation DD applies to deposit accounts, including checking accounts, and requires disclosures concerning account terms and fee schedules. Regulation DD also provides that a depository institution must provide account disclosures before an account is opened or before a service is provided, whichever is earlier, when a fee required to be disclosed is assessed. Because this currency exchange was funded from my checking account and may have involved account-based pricing, commission waivers, or foreign exchange service charges, Chase should identify the checking-account terms, fee schedule, foreign currency exchange disclosures, commission schedule, waiver terms, and any preferred-pricing provisions that applied. Because Chase failed to clearly disclose the true cost of the currency exchange, refused to unwind the transaction at the original rate, and instead offered a buy-back rate that would have caused an additional loss, I have lost confidence in Chases handling of my deposit-account services. I am considering closing my Chase accounts when I return from my trip.

The fraudulent charges consist of repeated XXXX transactions in XXXX, along with foreign exchange conversion fees, forming a consistent pattern across months. CRITICAL ISSUE NOT REASONABLY IDENTIFIABLE EARLIER : When the fraud began in XX/XX/XXXX, the transactions appeared as small XXXX charges intermixed with normal activity. Because XXXX is a merchant I legitimately use, these charges did not immediately appear suspicious. Additionally, the foreign nature of the transactions was not clearly obvious, as the XXXX currency and exchange rates were embedded within transaction details. The activity consisted of multiple low-value transactions rather than a single large suspicious charge. Only over time did a recognizable pattern emerge, including repeated foreign transactions, increasing frequency, and the absence of these transactions in my XXXX account. This was therefore a gradual and continuous fraud pattern that could not reasonably be identified at the beginning. BANK ACCOUNTABILITY AND FAILURE TO DETECT PATTERN : Chase was already aware of a prior card compromise when my original card was reported stolen and replaced. Despite this, the replacement card began showing repeated foreign XXXX transactions shortly afterward. These transactions followed a clear, repetitive pattern with consistent merchant, currency, and structure. The activity continued for an extended period without being flagged, blocked, or escalated by the bank. Financial institutions promote their fraud detection systems, yet this extended pattern of foreign activity went undetected and unflagged. INCONSISTENT TREATMENT OF IDENTICAL TRANSACTIONS : Chase has already acknowledged that some of these transactions are unauthorized by issuing partial reimbursement. The evidence demonstrates a continuous pattern of unauthorized foreign transactions that were not reasonably identifiable at the outset and must be treated as a single fraud scheme. I am concerned that disputed balances tied to unresolved unauthorized transaction claims are continuing to affect my ability to access banking services. I am requesting CFPB review regarding whether Wells Fargo : - Conducted reasonable investigations under Regulation E - Properly satisfied its burden of proving authorization under 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( b ) - Improperly treated unauthorized EFT disputes as merchant or merchandise disputes- Improperly reversed provisional credits without sufficient proof of authorization - Improperly maintained overdraft balances and fees arising from disputed unauthorized transactions - Improperly closed the account while disputed unauthorized transactions remained unresolved - Improperly reported disputed balances to XXXX XXXX XXXX or related systems

I am filing this formal complaint against Goldman Sachs Bank USA ( operating as Marcus by Goldman Sachs ) regarding an unannounced, abrupt modification to their transaction processing policies. This sudden operational change resulted in a failed credit card bill payment, exposing me to immediate financial penalties and potential damage to my credit rating. For several consecutive years, I have routinely and successfully paid my monthly credit card balances by initiating external ACH pull requests directly from my credit card issuers, drawn against my Marcus High-Yield Savings Account. Marcus has consistently, and without interruption, honored these transactions over a multi-year period, establishing a clear, stable operational history for my account. On XX/XX/year>, Marcus abruptly rejected a legitimate ACH debit payment initiated by my credit card issuer, doing so with zero prior notice, warning, or electronic communication. Upon contacting Marcus customer support to investigate the failed transfer, a corporate representative informed me that Marcus has implemented an internal policy change that " no longer allows transfers aside from to other personal checking or savings accounts owned by the client, '' effectively blocking all third-party ACH pulls for credit card bills. The customer service representative explicitly confirmed that no advance disclosure, notice of a change in terms, or warning banner was issued to account holders prior to implementing this highly restrictive shift. While I understand that financial institutions maintain internal discretion regarding fraud and risk parameters, Marcuss failure to provide an advance disclosure violates the spirit and core intent of Regulation DD ( Truth in Savings Act ) specifically 12 CFR 1030.5 ( a ), which mandates a minimum of 30 days ' advance written notice for any structural change that adversely affects the consumer or restricts their transaction capabilities. By failing to provide this mandatory notification window, Marcus denied me the necessary time to restructure my automated financial obligations, directly exposing me to late fees, returned check fees from my credit card company, and the threat of adverse reporting to credit bureaus.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX roughly a week after the accounts were opened, I received an email from Chase titled " Account update. The email stated, " Due to recent activity, or because we need more information from you, we have restricted your account ( s ) and may close it soon, '' and directed me to call XXXX. I called Chase. The representative told me that Chase 's terms and conditions allow the bank to terminate banking relationships at its discretion and that I would not be able to open new Chase deposit accounts. I was not given a specific reason for the closure. I was not told which database or flag triggered it. Chase has opened and then closed deposit accounts I applied for on more than one prior occasion. I value Chase as an institution and, given Chase 's national footprint, I am actively looking to transition my primary banking from the credit union I currently use to Chase. Disclosure of whether the closure was based on XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX, another consumer reporting agency, or Chase 's internal risk database. If an external consumer reporting agency was involved, I need to know which one so I can exercise my dispute rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. 4. ( 4 ) and ( 5 ), no claim for benefits awarded, adjudged or paid or any interest in the fund may be taken on account of any liability incurred by the party entitled thereto. '' XXXX XXXX XXXX is the party entitled to the unemployment insurance benefits deposited into Account # XXXX. The statute is unambiguous : no claim may be taken against her benefits on account of another person 's liability. The statutory exceptions in subsections ( 4 ) and ( 5 ) are narrow and exhaustive. Subsection ( 4 ) addresses child support withholding by the Department of Workforce Development. Subsection ( 5 ) addresses deductions permitted by federal law. The WI DOR levy for a third party 's state tax debt falls within neither exception. No exception applies here. The four unemployment insurance payments totaling {$1200.00} each clearly labeled " XXXX XXXX XXXX '' in the account ledger must be returned in full. B. Consumer complaint narrative: I am disputing Wells Fargo 's denial of my fraud claim for unauthorized electronic fund transfers from my checking and savings accounts on XX/XX/year>. On XX/XX/year>, my physical Wells Fargo debit card was stolen. The same day, before I discovered the theft, unauthorized transfers totaling {$5400.00} were initiated from two of my Wells Fargo accounts : Six unauthorized XXXX transfers totaling {$3500.00} - five from my savings account and one from my checking account. Three unauthorized XXXX XXXX debits totaling {$1800.00} from my checking account and two payments to UPG Paymentico for {$49.00} each funded via my stolen Wells Fargo debit card. I discovered the unauthorized activity on XX/XX/year> and immediately reported the stolen debit card and unauthorized transfers to Wells Fargo. I did not authorize, initiate, or consent to any of these transfers. I did not provide my card, PIN, banking credentials, or device to any third party. Wells Fargo denied my claim, stating the transactions came from a recognized device, matched my usual login pattern, and originated from my IP address. Wells Fargo reached this denial within 10 business days of my notification and did not provide provisional credit at any point. While 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ) permits a bank to forgo provisional credit if it completes its investigation within 10 business days, the speed of this denial- for nine unauthorized transactions across two accounts involving a stolen physical access device ( my debit card ) - raises serious concerns about the adequacy of the investigation. Additionally, Wells Fargo has failed to provide a written explanation of its denial findings, as required under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ). I learned of the denial only through a verbal communication during a telephone call I initiated. To date, Wells Fargo has not mailed or delivered any written explanation of its findings or any notice of my right to request the documents relied upon in making its determination. This is a separate procedural violation of Regulation E, independent of the merits of the denial itself. Also, Wells Fargo 's stated denial rationale does not meet the bank 's burden of proof under 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( b ), which requires the financial institution to prove that a disputed transfer was authorized. " Authorized '' under Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. 1005.2 ( m ) ) requires actual authority granted by the consumer. A thief in possession of a stolen access device does not have actual authority, regardless of whether transactions appear consistent with prior account activity. Wells Fargo 's assertion that the transactions matched my usual login pattern is also inconsistent with the actual activity. The unauthorized transactions included five rapid sequential XXXX transfers draining funds from a savings account - a pattern entirely unlike my prior account usage. A legitimate account holder does not typically empty savings via repeated XXXX transfers in rapid succession while simultaneously pushing funds to XXXX XXXX from checking. Wells Fargo 's fraud monitoring should have flagged this activity, and its failure to do so reflects inadequate fraud detection - not authorization by me. Device recognition, login pattern, and IP match establish only that the thief had sufficient access to bypass Wells Fargo 's fraud screens- not that I authorized the transfers. CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX makes clear that fraud-induced transfers, including account takeovers, are unauthorized electronic fund transfers under the EFTA. Because I reported the loss of my access device on the same day it was stolen, my maximum liability under 12 C.F.R. 1005.6 ( b ) ( 1 ) is {$50.00}. I request that Wells Fargo : -Reverse the denial of my claims. -Reinstate {$5400.00} to the affected accounts. -Provide all documents relied upon in reaching the denial determination, as required under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ) ( ii ), including but not limited to device identifiers, IP addresses, geolocation data, and transaction metadata for each of the nine disputed transactions. -Identify whether any new device was enrolled to either account between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/year>. -Provide the XXXX recipient information for each of the six transfers. -Provide the written explanation of findings required under 12 C.F.R. 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ), including notice of my right to request the documents relied upon in the determination.

Every record maintained by PNC account statements, 1099 forms, and all correspondence was directed to her Ohio address at XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX, OH XXXX. This inaccurate reporting potentially resulted in overstated taxable income attributed to the estate of XXXX XXXX. That the CFPB investigate PNC Bank 's handling of the XXXX XXXX estate accounts, including the unauthorized reductions, the improper escheatment, the unauthorized beneficiary changes, and the failure to produce records. 2. Consumer complaint narrative: I. SUMMARY OF COMPLAINT I am filing this complaint against Chime Financial , Inc. for multiple violations of Regulation E ( Electronic Fund Transfer Act, 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq. ) in connection with 14 unauthorized transfers totaling {$18000.00} from my Chime debit card account to XXXX, a company I have never used, recognized, or authorized transactions with. Chime has failed to provide provisional credit, failed to provide documentation supporting their denial, and has failed to conduct a adequate investigation as required by law. II. FACTS 1. I identified 14 unauthorized transactions on my Chime debit card account totaling {$18000.00}, all of which were transfers to XXXX a company I have never used or authorized to receive funds from my account. 2. I filed my initial fraud report on XX/XX/year>. Following this report, I received written communication from Chime stating : " You will receive a temporary credit if we are unable to resolve your dispute by XX/XX/year>. '' This communication constitutes an acknowledgment of my dispute and an implicit representation regarding provisional credit obligations. 3. On approximately XX/XX/year> before the stated XX/XX/XXXX resolution deadline Chime notified me by email that " We've completed our investigation and determined that no error occurred with the transaction ( s ) you disputed, '' without providing any documentation, evidence, or explanation to support this conclusion. 4. On that same day, I called Chime customer service and formally requested the documentation supporting their denial. I was told my case would be escalated and that I would receive a written response within 10 business days. No documentation was ever received. 5. On XX/XX/year>, I re-filed my fraud claim with additional supporting documentation, including evidence that my credentials were used without my authorization and that XXXX itself had frozen and subsequently shut down the account in question due to fraud concerns corroborating that these transactions were unauthorized. 6. During the XX/XX/XXXX call, I requested supporting documentation for the initial denial for a second time. No documentation was received. 7. I called again to request this documentation a third time. As of the date of this complaint, I have still not received any documentation whatsoever supporting Chime 's initial denial despite three separate requests. 8. As of the date of this complaint, it has been more than 10 business days since I re-filed my fraud claim on XX/XX/year>, and I have not received provisional credit. My appeal remains unresolved. III. REGULATORY VIOLATIONS VIOLATION XXXX : Failure to Provide Provisional Credit Within 10 Business Days 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) Regulation E requires a financial institution to provisionally credit a consumer 's account within 10 business days of receiving notice of an error if the investigation can not be completed within that timeframe. Chime 's own written communication acknowledged this obligation by referencing the XX/XX/XXXX resolution deadline. As of the date of this complaint, more than 10 business days have elapsed since both my initial XX/XX/XXXX filing and my XX/XX/XXXX refiling, and no provisional credit has been issued. This constitutes a clear violation of 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ). VIOLATION 2 : Failure to Provide Adequate Written Explanation of Denial 12 CFR 1005.11 ( d ) When a financial institution determines that no error occurred, Regulation E requires it to deliver a written explanation of its findings and inform the consumer of their right to request the documents relied upon in making that determination. Chime 's denial consisted solely of the statement " no error occurred '' with no explanation, no evidence, and no identification of what documents or factors were considered. This bare denial does not satisfy the written explanation requirement under 12 CFR 1005.11 ( d ). VIOLATION 3 : Failure to Provide Documents Upon Request 12 CFR 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ) Regulation E explicitly requires that upon consumer request, the financial institution provide copies of the documents it relied upon in its investigation. I have made this request on three separate occasions verbally on approximately XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and a subsequent call and have received no documents whatsoever. This repeated failure to comply with my documented requests constitutes a violation of 12 CFR 1005.11 ( d ) ( 1 ). VIOLATION 4 : Failure to Conduct a Reasonable Investigation 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ) Regulation E requires that a financial institution conduct a reasonable investigation of a reported error. The fact that Chime closed my initial investigation before the deadline it had itself communicated, without providing any supporting evidence, and in the face of substantial corroborating evidence including XXXX 's own account freeze and closure due to fraud concerns raises serious questions about whether a reasonable investigation was conducted. A bona fide investigation would weigh third-party corroboration of fraud. VIOLATION 5 : Failure to Acknowledge Re-Filed Claim With Provisional Credit 12 CFR 1005.11 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) Upon re-filing on XX/XX/year> with additional supporting documentation, a new 10-business-day provisional credit clock was triggered. More than 10 business days have now elapsed since that filing with no provisional credit issued, constituting an independent violation separate from the initial claim. IV. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE AVAILABLE - Written email from Chime referencing provisional credit and XX/XX/XXXX resolution deadline - Written denial email from Chime stating " no error occurred '' - Documentation of re-filed claim on XX/XX/year> with supporting materials - Evidence of XXXX account freeze and closure due to fraud concerns - Account statements showing 14 unauthorized transactions totaling {$18000.00} XXXX respectfully request that the CFPB investigate this matter and compel Chime to comply with its obligations under Regulation E. The amount at issue {$18000.00} represents a significant financial harm, and Chime 's repeated failure to provide documentation, provisional credit, or an adequate investigation has left me without recourse or transparency.

Consumer complaint narrative: To Whom It May Concern, Thank you for your response regarding my CFPB complaint. At no point during the interaction was I informed that a XXXX security freeze or credit-related restriction was preventing verification. Instead, the process appeared disorganized and unclear, leaving us without a meaningful explanation while in the branch. Second, I want to clarify that a XXXX security freeze is a consumer protection mechanism, not evidence of wrongdoing or credit repair activity in any negative sense. Characterizing it in that manner is misleading. Consumers place freezes on reporting agencies specifically to protect themselves from identity theft and fraud. Many financial institutions are able to handle this situation by either : informing the customer of the freeze and allowing temporary removal, using alternate verification methods, or resuming the application once verification is completed. Your response indicates Frost Bank had no alternative process whatsoever. If that is truly Frosts policy, then the concern becomes whether customers are being properly informed upfront that Frost can not accommodate standard consumer security protections during account opening. Additionally, the explanation that an error in the XXXXXXXX response prevented account opening conflicts somewhat with the later statement that the issue was likely caused by a freeze. These are materially different explanations : an error implies a technical or systems failure, whereas a freeze implies an expected security restriction. I would appreciate clarification as to which specifically occurred. For completeness, I am requesting : Confirmation of the exact verification response Frost Bank received from XXXX ; Clarification as to whether the application was denied, unable to be processed, or voluntarily abandoned ; A copy of any adverse action or compliance notice associated with this event, if applicable ; Clarification of Frost Banks policy regarding applicants with XXXX freezes in place ; Confirmation that no negative internal banking notation or risk designation was placed on my profile as a result of this interaction. My primary concern remains the lack of transparency and the inconsistent explanation provided both during the branch visit and in the subsequent response. I believe consumers should be clearly informed when a security freeze is the reason verification can not proceed, rather than being left uncertain about whether they were denied for some other reason. I look forward to your clarification. Sincerely, XXXX XXXX XXXX

Thereafter, I received a written notice from Wells Fargo stating that the bank was denying my fraud claim and closing the matter. The denial letter did not provide meaningful factual findings, supporting documentation, transaction evidence, surveillance evidence, device records, or any detailed explanation showing how Wells Fargo concluded that the transaction was authorized. Despite my immediate contact to Wells Fargo again I disputed the denial decision because I do not agree with the banks conclusion and believe the investigation was unreasonable and inadequate. I requested further review but have no trust in their statements. Basis for CFPB Complaint : I believe based on competent research that Wells Fargo violated the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ), 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq., and Regulation E, 12 C.F.R. 1005.11, by failing to conduct a reasonable good-faith investigation into this unauthorized electronic fund transfer. Specifically : Wells Fargo failed to provide competent evidence establishing that I authorized the transaction. The mere fact that a PIN may have been used or that the card number was utilized does not prove authorization. Modern fraud schemes frequently involve : card skimming, card cloning, compromised merchant terminals, unauthorized digital wallet access, account takeover fraud, stolen credentials, or other electronic compromise methods. My physical debit card remained in my possession at all times. Wells Fargo failed to provide the evidence relied upon in denying the claim. The denial letter failed to include : transaction metadata ; ATM or merchant surveillance evidence ; device identification records ; IP address logs ; geolocation information ; chip-read verification data ; fraud analyst findings ; investigative notes ; merchant authentication records ; or any meaningful documentation demonstrating that the transaction was actually authorized by me. Wells Fargo appears to have conducted only a superficial or automated investigation. Based upon the limited response provided, Wells Fargo appears to have denied the claim without : interviewing me in detail; reviewing objective fraud indicators; comparing my normal transaction behavior ; determining whether the transaction location was consistent with my physical location ; or evaluating whether the transaction reflected potential card compromise or account takeover activity. Wells Fargo improperly shifted the burden onto me. Under Regulation E, Wells Fargo bears the responsibility to conduct a reasonable investigation and determine whether the transfer was authorized. I should not be forced to prove a negative where the bank itself possesses the transaction data, surveillance access, authentication logs, and fraud detection tools necessary to evaluate the dispute properly. Wells Fargo failed to provide transparency concerning the investigation. I request that Wells Fargo be required to provide : all documents relied upon in denying the claim ; copies of investigative findings ; all electronic transaction logs ; ATM or merchant records ; authentication and access logs ; fraud detection analysis ; and any evidence purportedly showing authorization. Requested Resolution I respectfully request that the CFPB require Wells Fargo to : Reopen and conduct a full and reasonable Regulation E investigation ; Provide all documents and evidence relied upon in denying the claim ; Reimburse the unauthorized {$1000.00} withdrawal ; Refund any associated fees or charges ; Confirm whether the transaction involved : ATM withdrawal, debit card purchase, electronic transfer, digital wallet transaction, or another payment mechanism ; Preserve all surveillance footage, electronic logs, and fraud investigation materials related to this matter ; and Ensure compliance with federal consumer protection obligations under the EFTA and Regulation E. Consumer complaint narrative: NFCU is holding a legitimate legal settlement check issued by the law firm XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, repeatedly resetting the availability clock without legal justification, and hiding the funds from my account ledger. Friday, XX/XX/year> : I deposited the settlement check at an NFCU branch. Saturday, XX/XX/year> : The funds cleared and showed as " Available '' Sunday, XX/XX/year> : NFCU locked the account due to an automated " Fraud Activity '' flag Monday, XX/XX/year> : I visited a physical branch. Staff unlocked the account but stated the back office placed a new 5-day hold starting that day. No written receipt or hold notice was provided. Monday, XX/XX/year> ( At XXXX XXXX ) : Following the branch 's instructions to escalate, I called the phone support line and spoke directly with a supervisor. The supervisor verbally informed me that they were manually placing another 5-day security hold on my funds starting at that moment. Crucially, the supervisor explicitly stated on the recorded line that " there is no reason listed on the account system '' for this hold. Abuse of Exception Holds ( 229.13 ) : A financial institution can not repeatedly alter or extend a hold timeline within the same day without a valid, lawful reason ( such as reasonable cause to doubt collectibility ). A supervisor admitting that " no reason is listed '' proves this hold is entirely arbitrary and non-compliant. Failure to Provide Statutory Written Notice ( 229.13 ( g ) ) : NFCU has failed to provide a physical or digital Hold Notice detailing the specific reason for the hold and a firm availability date. Total Lack of Ledger Transparency : The deposited funds do not appear anywhere on my online banking profilenot as available, pending, or held. NFCU has effectively scrubbed the funds from my view, blocking my ability to track my own property. Denial of Documentation : The branch staff refused or failed to provide me with any physical printouts, deposit receipts, or a statutory written Hold Notice detailing the security hold. Disappearance of Funds : As of today, the deposited settlement funds do not show up on my online account ledger at all. The funds have completely disappeared from my available balance. Only shows pending transaction history, effectively hiding my money without my consent or a tracking trail. Under Regulation CC ( 229.13 ), a financial institution is legally required to provide a consumer with a written or digital Hold Notice specifying the exact reason for a hold and a firm availability date. Withholding a deposit from view and failing to issue a transaction receipt violates federal banking transparency standards.

The affected account is an investment account with a balance in the mid-six figures. Changes of XXXXl XXXX XXXX over days or weeks are common in an investment portfolio of this size and could reasonably be attributed to normal market fluctuations. I was also unaware that my debit card was linked to this investment account. I had always used my checking account for my everyday purchases, and I rarely used this debit card. I understood that the investment account was intended primarily for investing, and I would access those funds only if I specifically needed to do so. Throughout the investigation, I repeatedly requested an explanation regarding how and why the debit card was linked to this investment account but did not receive a substantive response. The unauthorized activity followed clear and repetitive patterns involving a small number of merchants. One merchant alone accounted for 137 debit card charges totaling {$4100.00}, including as many as eight transactions in a single day, with recurring dollar amounts and purchase-and-return activity. Another merchant accounted for 50 debit card charges, including 14 transactions in a single day. Additional merchants accounted for 35, 19, and 12 debit card charges, respectively, each exhibiting repeated transaction patterns over short periods. A summary of these transaction patterns is attached. Shortly after I reported the fraud, JPMorgan reimbursed {$850.00}, representing only the most recent unauthorized transactions that the bank determined were eligible for reimbursement. The remaining unauthorized transactions continued under investigation for several months. During that time, I fully cooperated with every request made by the bank, including reviewing each transaction and identifying which transactions were authorized and unauthorized. I also repeatedly requested an explanation regarding the banks fraud investigation, the absence of fraud alerts or intervention, the linkage of my debit card to my investment account, and the basis for the reimbursement decision. After approximately five months of investigation, JPMorgan ultimately denied reimbursement for the remaining unauthorized transactions, stating that I was responsible for reviewing my account statements. I respectfully disagree with that determination. While I understand the importance of monitoring my accounts, I also believe banks have an important role in monitoring and investigating unusual account activity. In this case, the bank determined that a portion of the unauthorized transactions warranted reimbursement, yet denied reimbursement for the remaining unauthorized transactions arising from the same prolonged pattern of activity. Despite months of investigation, I have not received a satisfactory explanation regarding the repetitive transaction patterns, the absence of fraud alerts or intervention, the linkage of my debit card to my investment account, or the basis for denying reimbursement for the earlier unauthorized transactions. I respectfully request that the CFPB review JPMorgans handling of my fraud claim and assist in obtaining reimbursement for the remaining unauthorized debit card transactions. Complaint Based on Newly Discovered Evidence I am submitting this complaint based on documentary evidence that I discovered after the CFPB closed my previous complaint. This complaint concerns Navy Federal Credit Unions seizure of an amended federal income tax refund that belonged solely to XXXX XXXX XXXX. This is not a dispute over XXXX XXXX general contractual right to offset funds belonging to me. The issue is whether XXXX XXXX had the legal authority to seize funds belonging to another individual after its own records established that individual was no longer a joint owner of the receiving account. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX originally filed his XXXX federal income tax return through XXXX. At that time, the refund was properly deposited into my Navy Federal checking account because that account information was on file through XXXX processing bank. XXXX later filed an amended federal tax return ( XXXX XXXX ). He reasonably expected the amended refund to be mailed to him. Immediately upon receipt of the deposit, Navy Federal withdrew virtually the entire amount and applied it toward debts owed solely by me. Newly Discovered Evidence After my previous CFPB complaint was closed, I located Navy Federals official XX/XX/XXXX account statement. That statement clearly identifies my checking account as having : Joint Owner ( s ) : NONE This evidence establishes that XXXX XXXX XXXX was not a joint owner of my account when his amended federal tax refund was deposited and seized. This evidence was not available when I submitted my prior complaint. IRS Documentation The IRS documents establish that the amended refund belonged exclusively to XXXX XXXX XXXX. Specifically : * The IRS XXXX notice is addressed only to XXXX XXXX XXXX. * The amended Form XXXX was filed solely under XXXX XXXX XXXX Social Security number. * My name does not appear anywhere on the amended return. * The IRS determined that XXXX XXXX XXXX was entitled to the amended refund. These documents establish that the refund belonged to XXXX XXXX XXXX and not to me. Contradiction in Navy Federals Position After the seizure, I contacted Navy Federal and was informed by representatives that the funds could be seized because XXXX had previously been a joint owner of my account. Neither explanation addresses the central issue. The question is not whether Navy Federal may offset funds belonging to me. The question is whether Navy Federal had the legal authority to treat XXXX XXXX XXXX amended federal income tax refund as my property after its own records established he was no longer a joint owner of the account receiving the deposit. Relief Requested I respectfully request that the CFPB require Navy Federal Credit Union to answer the following questions : 1. What legal authority permitted Navy Federal to seize an amended federal income tax refund issued solely to XXXX XXXX XXXX? 2. Why does Navy Federals XX/XX/XXXX account statement identify Joint Owner ( s ) : NONE if the company contends XXXX prior ownership justified the seizure? 3. Why did Navy Federal fail to address the ownership of the deposited funds in its previous CFPB response? 4. If Navy Federal maintains that it lawfully seized XXXX XXXX XXXX refund, please identify the specific contractual provision, federal regulation, or state law that authorized it to apply funds belonging to XXXX XXXX XXXX toward debts owed solely by me. Citibank is thus mailing a 29-year customer formal notices that state he failed to provide " critical, missing information '' and threaten to liquidate his retirement account, while simultaneously instructing him to ignore those notices because nothing is in fact outstanding. Consumer complaint narrative: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Complaint I am submitting this complaint regarding the handling of a fraud incident involving my accounts and my daughter 's accounts by Randolph-Brooks Federal Credit Union ( RBFCU ). At the time of this incident, a total of {$18000.00} was held across five accounts belonging to me and my daughter. On XX/XX/year>, I received a phone call that appeared to originate from RBFCU 's XXXX XXXX, Texas phone number. The caller identified himself as " XXXX '' from RBFCU and stated that there was suspicious activity on my account originating from XXXX, Georgia. He asked whether I had authorized any transactions from that location. I responded that I had not and that I wanted to dispute any unauthorized activity. During the call, the individual provided personal information that appeared to verify he was associated with my bank, including my account information, date of birth, Social Security number, and the answer to my account security question. When I expressed concern about providing information over the phone, I specifically stated that I would not give out my personal information. The caller responded that RBFCU would never ask me to provide personal information and that he was simply reviewing suspicious activity. The caller placed me on hold several times while claiming to investigate and dispute transactions. He then provided what he described as a fraud claim number ( Case No. ____________ ) and scheduled a follow-up appointment for the following day. He informed me that my online banking access would be unavailable for 24 to 48 hours while the fraud investigation was being processed, but stated that our debit cards would continue to work. On XX/XX/year>, the caller contacted me again and informed me that my account had been compromised. He stated that an unauthorized individual had obtained my account number and routing number and that I would need to establish a new account. He advised me that funds had been moved in three transactions : {$5000.00}, {$5000.00}, and {$5900.00}. The caller instructed me to log into my online banking account. When I did so, I discovered that my daughter 's checking account, my daughter 's savings account, and my savings account had all been reduced to XXXX. My checking account showed a balance of {$15000.00}, which did not equal the total amount that had previously existed across our five accounts. Based on the balances that existed before the incident, approximately {$18000.00} should have been present across those accounts. This means that approximately {$2800.00} was unaccounted for at the time I reviewed the balances. This discrepancy further increased my concern that unauthorized transactions had occurred and that funds were missing from our accounts. At this point I was in a state of panic and believed I was working directly with an RBFCU fraud representative. The caller instructed me to verify my username and then directed me to process transfers involving the amounts he had identified. He represented these actions as necessary steps to move funds into a new secure account. He then scheduled another appointment for XX/XX/year>, to establish new account information. No one from RBFCU contacted me on XX/XX/XXXX as promised. I attempted to call the credit union but was unable to remain on hold because of work obligations. Later that evening, my daughter informed me that her debit card no longer worked and that neither of us could access our online banking. On XX/XX/year>, I contacted RBFCU and explained what had occurred. I was informed by an employee that RBFCU would never call customers in the manner I described regarding fraud activity. She asked whether I had provided my username and indicated that customers should never provide that information. However, during the same conversation she immediately requested my username to verify my account, which I found confusing and inconsistent. I was then transferred to the fraud department where a fraud claim was opened. The representative informed me that one transaction had already been flagged as suspicious and that I might be able to recover those funds. However, she did not obtain a complete statement regarding the events that occurred, did not ask for a detailed timeline, did not provide meaningful guidance regarding securing my accounts, did not offer assistance opening replacement accounts, and did not explain how I could regain access to my online banking. On XX/XX/year>, I contacted RBFCU again and spoke with a fraud department employee named XXXX. I informed him that a fraud claim had been opened the previous day. After reviewing my account, XXXX initially stated, " Ma'am, there is no fraud claim on this account. '' I then provided him with the fraud claim number I had been given. Only after I supplied the case number did he acknowledge that a claim existed and state that he could see it in the system. During that conversation XXXX asked me to answer my account security question. He informed me that my answer was incorrect. He then changed my security question to a new one. This raised serious concerns because the answer I provided had previously been correct. The fact that my security question had apparently been altered suggests that unauthorized changes may have been made to my account security settings. At no point during the conversation did XXXX address how or when the security question had been changed, who had changed it, or whether this indicated additional unauthorized access to my account. I also asked XXXX whether my daughter needed to open a separate fraud claim because her accounts had also been affected. XXXX specifically advised that she did not need to file her own claim because our accounts were linked. However, when my daughter later visited RBFCU on two separate occasions, two different employees informed her that she should have opened her own fraud claim. This conflicting information created confusion and raises concerns regarding whether her losses were properly documented and investigated. During the same call, XXXX instructed me to open a new checking account and a new savings account, which I did. I asked where any recovered funds or reimbursement would be deposited once the investigation concluded. XXXX responded that the funds would go into " either one '' of the accounts but did not provide a clear answer, confirmation, or documentation regarding where reimbursement funds would be deposited. Additionally, despite the fact that I repeatedly explained that I was unable to access my accounts, XXXX did not provide meaningful assistance in restoring my online banking access or helping me regain control of my accounts. On XX/XX/year>, I sent a detailed written statement to RBFCU 's fraud department outlining my concerns regarding the incident and investigation. In that communication, I explained that I disagreed with any characterization of this matter as merely a scam in which I voluntarily authorized transactions. I explained that the caller possessed sensitive account information before I ever disclosed my username and appeared to have access to information that should not have been available to an unauthorized individual. I am concerned that unauthorized access to my account occurred before I disclosed any information and I request that the credit union investigate whether an account compromise, security failure, or other unauthorized access event occurred. Throughout this process I have received conflicting information from multiple RBFCU employees regarding the existence of my fraud claim, account security changes, whether my daughter required her own claim, and how reimbursement funds would be handled. These inconsistencies have made it extremely difficult to understand the status of the investigation and have undermined my confidence in the credit union 's handling of this matter. My concerns include the following : 1. RBFCU did not obtain a complete statement regarding the fraudulent activity before beginning its investigation. 2. RBFCU employees provided inconsistent and contradictory information regarding account security, fraud reporting requirements, and investigation procedures. 3. I was not provided timely or adequate assistance in securing my accounts or regaining access to my banking services. 4. My daughter and I were left without reliable access to our accounts and banking services. 5. Apparently unauthorized changes were made to my account security settings, including my security question, and these changes were not adequately investigated or explained. 6. I am concerned that RBFCU may be improperly treating these transactions as authorized solely because I was deceived by an individual impersonating a bank employee. 7. I request confirmation that RBFCU is conducting a full Regulation E investigation into all unauthorized electronic fund transfers associated with this incident. 8. I request that RBFCU provide any provisional credit required under Regulation E while the investigation remains pending. 9. I request a full accounting of all transactions, account changes, security setting modifications, login activity, and investigative findings related to this incident. I respectfully request that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau review RBFCU 's handling of this matter, ensure that a thorough investigation is conducted, and require the credit union to provide a clear explanation of its findings and compliance with applicable consumer protection laws and Regulation E requirements. Thank you for your assistance. XXXX XXXX

Consumer complaint narrative: PORTAL NARRATIVE U.S. Bank Official Check # XXXX U.S. Bank 's fraud and risk reporting infrastructure contains a structural blind spot : named payees on active official checks have no recognized standing to report risk to the issuing bank. The third-party remitter controls all remedies. The payee, whose name and address are physically printed on the instrument, is invisible to the bank 's intake system. This complaint documents what happens when that gap meets a live instrument with a compromised custody history and a payee who had no way to protect her identity. The underlying transaction was an entity disbursement. I am not asking the CFPB to review the originating entity 's internal governance, administrative rights, or entitlement to funds. I am strictly asking the CFPB to review what U.S. Bank did and failed to do after one of its own official checks entered circulation bearing my identity. What Happened Official Check # XXXX was issued in my name on XX/XX/year>, and mailed via regular USPS First-Class Mail without tracking, without mailing confirmation, and without my knowledge or consent. I was not consulted about how the instrument would be sent. I was not informed until it was already in circulation. A {$5000.00} negotiable instrument bearing my legal name and mailing address entered the public mail stream with zero accountability infrastructure and zero input from the person whose identity was on it. It never arrived. On XX/XX/year> On Day 15 following issuance, I contacted U.S. Bank 's Fraud Liaison Unit not to obtain account information, but to provide it. The Fraud Liaison refused to open a case. No check number was requested. No intake occurred. No mechanism existed for a named payee to submit risk information about an active instrument bearing her own identity. I then filed reports with the USPS Postal Inspection Service and local law enforcement. On XX/XX/year> I executed a notarized Affidavit of Non-Receipt and Non-Negotiation and presented it personally at a U.S. Bank branch in XXXX, California. No intake occurred. XX/XX/XXXX XX/XX/year> I contacted multiple U.S. Bank personnel by email. No substantive response was received. On XX/XX/year> I was informed by the originating remitter without documentation that the instrument had been returned to sender, that a stop-payment had been initiated, that the stop-payment had been reversed, and that the same compromised instrument had been re-mailed. I was not asked. I was not notified in advance. I can not help but consider whether earlier bank intervention, had any reporting mechanism existed, might have prevented that second circulation entirely. The bank 's structural blind spot removed the only friction that might have stopped it. When the instrument arrived by Certified Mail on XX/XX/XXXX, I was handed an impossible choice. Accept it and contradict my sworn affidavit, waive all objections to the 29-day custody gap, and absorb every unresolved risk alone. Or refuse it, and watch the instrument re-enter circulation, my PII remain exposed, and control return to the party that created the problem. I refused. There was no option that protected me. On XX/XX/year> I contacted the Fraud Liaison Unit again. Still no meaningful intake occurred. Later that day, I reached branch personnel directly at the issuing location for the first time. I submitted affidavits, police reports, USPIS confirmation, and a complete chronology. U.S. Bank 's Executive Communications unit acknowledged receipt twice, in identical language, and provided no substantive response either time. The Harm I can not prove the instrument was intercepted, copied, or washed during those 29 days. Neither can anyone else. That uncertainty does not resolve in my favor ; it lives on my shoulders indefinitely. I am not the bank 's account holder. I am not the remitter. I am the person whose legal name and address are printed on a {$5000.00} negotiable instrument that floated untracked and unsecured through the public mail stream for nearly a month without my consent and without any mechanism for me to report the risk. If my PII was compromised during that window, no replacement check cures it. No cancellation retrieves a photographed document. No internal electronic status change eliminates the risk the physical paper continues to represent. The instrument is currently in transit back to the originating party. It has sat processing at a USPS facility since XX/XX/XXXX. When it arrives, I have no visibility into what happens next. The same parties who sent it untracked the first time, who facilitated re-circulation without documentation or payee consent, will have it back in their possession. Nothing has changed structurally to prevent this cycle from repeating. My exposure is not past tense. It is ongoing and I have no mechanism to stop it. I made contact with U.S. Bank across every available channelFraud Liaison, branch walk-in, multiple emails, a second Fraud Liaison call, direct branch contact at the issuing location, and Executive Communications escalation across nearly two months. I filed law enforcement reports. I executed a sworn affidavit. I submitted documentation at the bank 's own request. I did everything available to me. U.S. Bank has never confirmed whether any of it mattered. SEE ATTACHED DOCUMENT " FULL_COMPLAINT_TEXT.PDF '' FOR EVIDENCE AND EXHIBITS.

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) Formal Complaint I. Company and Product Information Company Concerned : Axos XXXX Product/Service : Checking / Savings Account II. Description of the Issue This complaint is formally filed to address Axos Bank 's unauthorized local ledger tampering, abrupt account closure, and the unlawful manual reversal of a {$980000.00} pre-funded cash item drawn on the Federal Reserve Bank of XXXX XXXX. Furthermore, this complaint addresses Axos XXXX XXXX failure to adhere to explicit clearing and routing instructions printed on the face of the instrument, resulting in the unlawful withholding of trust assets, deprivation of accrued interest, and actionable regulatory violations including fraudulent conversion, bank fraud, wire fraud, violation of UCC Article 3, and wrongful dishonor under established legal precedent. III. Statement of Facts & Timeline Trust Entity Legal Status : The claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is the lawful trustee of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a statutory business trust legally registered and organized under the laws of the State of Ohio. The trust is validated by an official certificate issued by Ohio Secretary of State XXXX XXXX, under Document Number : XXXX, with an effective date of XX/XX/XXXX. Specific Instrument Details : The transaction in question involves check number XXXX, dated XX/XX/XXXX, in the amount of {$980000.00}. This negotiable instrument was legally drawn on the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX via the Federal Reserve Bank of XXXX XXXX. Explicit Processing Instructions : The instrument carried an explicit, legally binding administrative instruction printed in the memo line : " Please process this payment as ACH only. '' System Acknowledgment & Deposit Alert : Upon presentation, Axos XXXX XXXX automated clearing systems scanned the instrument, verified the underlying routing and account data, and recognized the pre-funded asset. The system instantly credited the ledger, which successfully triggered a pre-set automated account alert for deposits exceeding {$500000.00}, confirming the funds had hit the account. Failure to Follow Routing Instructions : Despite the clear directive to clear the transaction strictly through the Automated Clearing House ( ACH ) electronic network, Axos Bank failed to route the item accordingly. Instead, after the automated system credited the balance, the bank 's back-office operations manually intervened. Unauthorized Ledger Manipulation : Rather than executing the transfer according to standard electronic clearing regulations, Axos XXXX personnel implemented a manual override. Direct screenshot evidence of the account ledger explicitly documents this local manipulation, displaying the initial {$980000.00} credit immediately followed by unauthorized manual reversals of negative {$980000.00} and negative {$970000.00}, leaving a manipulated local balance of {$10.00}. Formal Legal Demand ( XX/XX/XXXX ) : A three-page formal legal notice titled " RE : Immediate demand for release and correction of unlawfully reversed official check number XXXX '' was sent via USPS Certified Mail with tracking directly to the Axos XXXX Legal Department XXXX This letter explicitly placed the financial institution on formal notice regarding the unauthorized ledger manipulation and demanded immediate correction, an administrative remedy which Axos Bank completely ignored. Depository Bank Violation, Closed Loop Mechanics, & Legal Precedent : As a depository-only institution, Axos XXXX XXXX sole regulatory authority was to accept and route the item per its explicit instructions. The Federal Reserve Bank system operates strictly as a closed loop network ; consequently, the Federal Reserve Bank is the sole authority capable of issuing a transaction return code of any kind. The fact that the {$980000.00} deposit successfully settled and hit the account ledger conclusively proves that the Federal Reserve Bank did not issue a return code, nor did it recall, reject, or reverse the payment. Had the paying bank declined settlement, the funds would never have entered the account. Because this transaction was a pre-funded cash item, once the funds hit the account ledger, settlement was immediate, final, and legally irrevocable. By overriding this finalized transaction, Axos XXXX internally and manually bypassed standard clearing networks. Axos XXXX has engaged in fraudulent conversion, bank fraud, and wire fraud via their electronic communications network. Their actions represent a severe violation of UCC Article 3 ( specifically UCC 3-104 and 3-310 ( b ) ) governing the discharge and conditional effect of negotiable instruments. Furthermore, this constitutes a wrongful dishonor of a valid negotiable instrument in direct violation of established Supreme Court precedent laid out in Federal Reserve Bank of XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX ), which governs the duties and liabilities of collecting and depository banks handling cash items. Axos XXXX internally stripped the pre-loaded funds from the local ledger and subsequently terminated the banking relationship to withhold the asset. IV. Desired Resolution 1. Immediate Account Restoration : Reopen the closed Axos Bank account immediately and cease all unauthorized administrative or ledger tampering. 2. Full Restitution of Funds plus Accrued Interest : Correct the local ledger errors and restore the full {$980000.00} principal balance to the account, plus all applicable statutory or market-rate interest accrued on these withheld funds for the entire duration of the unlawful holding period ( exceeding one year ). 3. Production of Metadata Files & Audit Trail : Mandate that Axos Bank produce all electronic metadata files associated with this payment transaction. The CFPB must specifically pull these backend files to audit and verify the ISP spray and the Image Reference Number ( IRN ). This forensic verification will demonstrate the absolute absence of a valid Federal Reserve Bank return code, definitively establishing that Axos XXXX received, intercepted, and held the finalized funds. 4. Regulatory Accountability : Hold Axos XXXX strictly liable for failing to follow explicit ACH processing instructions, executing unauthorized manual ledger manipulation, committing fraudulent conversion and electronic wire/bank fraud, violating UCC Article 3 rules, violating Federal Reserve closed-loop clearing rules, and unlawfully withholding a finalized Federal Reserve cash item in violation of Federal Reserve Bank vXXXX XXXX XXXX My current Phone # is XXXX Please correct my Phone number in your system it wont allow me to change it.
